We examine multiple chiral supersymmetry-breaking scenarios in four-dimensional N=1 gauge theories, including theories such as SU(5) with a single anti-fundamental representation, SU(4) with two fundamental and one anti-fundamental representations, and SU(3) with three fundamental and one anti-fundamental representation. In each scenario, we establish a non-supersymmetric dual partner, similar to MONOPOLE OPERATIONS. By analyzing these dualities, we explore the effects of a non-supersymmetric dual on the monopole operators and an extensive set of observables in the SU(5) theory. Furthermore, we identify a novel monopole operator in the SU(5) theory that emerges from a non-supersymmetric dual, revealing novel dynamics and an extensive set of new interactions. Lastly, we outline a future research direction in the area of non-supersymmetric dualities.

A linear complementary set of group codes is defined as a collection of group codes that, when combined, form a complementary matrix with entries from a given principal ideal domain (PID). Given a PID with the property that its quotient by the square of its greatest common divisor divides the PID, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition ensuring the existence of a linear complementary set of group codes with specified parameters. This condition, expressed in terms of the code indices, aligns with a previously established result for linear complementary sets of linear codes. Furthermore, a linear complementary set of group codes of certain rank-zero codes induces a linear complementary set of the code's extension. Additionally, a linear complementary set of group codes of certain parameters is constructed using a specific type of PID. These results complement existing findings concerning linear complementary sets of group codes.

In this research, we present an efficient method for describing a agent's actions within a graphical model, allowing for straightforward representation of a utility function that is consistent with a given set of observations. This simplified representation makes it possible to exactiy compute the maximum joint probability estimation (MPE) for a smaller representation of the model and thus a limited optimization on the original one. We achieve this MPE computation through the application of two established methods: a full optimization for MPE and a within-a-cycle search. We also propose a variant of the message passing algorithm, which enables direct computation of MPE values within a single cycle of iteration. We evaluate the performance of our suggested description method, as well as the modified message passing algorithm, on a diverse set of instances that consist of large graphical models with simplified representations and smaller or larger MPE representations.

A study has been conducted to advance the field of visual and audio information fusion in a mobile robot navigation system designed for a studio-like environment. The research centers on creating an audio-visual localizing system for an item that can switch between being visible and sound-capable. When the item is visible, the system determines the item's location using a single camera. A depth sensor or three-dimensional point cloud data can be used to calculate the camera's viewing direction and the item's distance from the camera. The resulting 2D location is achieved through a simple calculation. When the item is out of sight but audible, the system relies on audio fusion to pinpoint the item's location. A camera records video of the studio while remaining fixed in the environment, and when the item is audible, image processing techniques are used to create a depth map. The item's 3D location is calculated by combining the depth map with the viewing direction from an accompanying audio recording. A color-based identification method is then employed to verify the calculated 3D data against the actual item dimensions and possible sound source locations. Experimental findings indicate that the proposed system accurately locates the item with a relatively low error margin even when the item is audible but not visible.

One of the main factors influencing the flow resistance of complex shapes is the dynamic interaction between flow and surface features. This interaction can lead to increased flow resistance in specific geometric configurations where flow is slowed relative to idealized shapes. In most cases, this phenomenon is observed in complex shapes with multiple features, but recent studies have demonstrated that even simple shapes with a single projection can experience increased flow resistance in certain orientations. A comprehensive study was conducted to better understand the dynamics of this flow resistance phenomenon, involving a range of shapes with a single projection across various materials and orientations. The research found that a critical parameter determines whether a shape will experience increased flow resistance or not, and this parameter is influenced by both the shape's structure and its orientation relative to the flow. The study further revealed that the dynamic transition process leading to increased flow resistance is consistent across different shapes and can be described using a unified scaling law. Additionally, the research showed that the resistance increase is more pronounced in situations where the flow interacts intensely with the shape's surface features. Based on these findings, the researchers proposed a theoretical explanation for the observed dynamics, which involves the collective effect of flow and shape surface features.

This study investigates hourly electricity consumption utilizing daily peak hours in Ghana. The capital's peak hours are defined as hours when electricity usage exceeds certain thresholds. The paper estimates peak hour patterns across various districts in Ghana's capital, analyzing factors such as seasonality, weather, and holidays. A Gaussian Mixture Model and the Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average model are employed to forecast hourly peaks. The results indicate that Akwidaa has the lowest peak hour penetration rate among all districts in Greater Accra. The study discovers that Teshie's peak hour pattern exhibits stronger autocorrelation than Akwidaa's, and that both Teshie and Akwidaa experience heightened peak hour penetrations during wet seasons and holidays. The findings suggest that Teshie's load behavior exhibits greater responsiveness to local weather and holidays than Akwidaa's behavior. The study predicts that both loads will experience increased peak hour penetrations during periods of high voltage.

A significant challenge in information science research is to measure the extent of peer review oversight. An innovative approach has been developed to quantify this issue by analyzing the connections between search queries, web content, and links generated by online search engines, particularly Google. This study is the first to demonstrate that search engines can fail to retrieve relevant information due to user preferences, thus highlighting the importance of considering these biases in academic publishing and bibliometric studies. A comprehensive dataset was employed, comprising 21 million search queries, 260 million web pages, and 1.09 billion links. The data analysis revealed a substantial underscoring of pertinent information by Google's algorithm, with estimates suggesting around 7% to 9% of relevant documents remain undiscovered. The complexity of this problem is shown to be an NP-complete issue, making it inevitable that a portion of relevant information will be overlooked even with optimal algorithms. Consequently, the development of more effective linking algorithms is proposed to mitigate the limitations of current search engines and enhance the discovery of online content.

Automatically creating code from visual representations is essential for addressing the digital gap and comprehending program equivalence, which is linked to long-standing open issues in software testing. Existing studies typically focus on structured inputs and utilize recognition-based models, which are unsuitable for handling complex, graph-based inputs like flow diagrams used in program generation. To address this challenge, we introduce GRCNN, a novel deep learning model that recognizes graphs within images and has been successful in generating programs from these visual representations. The proposed architecture combines the strengths of convolutional and recurrent networks to analyze visual and semantic program structures, while leveraging graph edges to model program flow. By employing a program-aware graph embedding layer, GRCNN is able to synthesize program graphs that conform to the program's structural framework. Our experiments conduct a detailed evaluation of the proposed model, which achieves exceptional results in program generation, surpassing the performance of the existing state-of-the-art baseline model by a significant margin. Additionally, an in-depth analysis presents various approaches to apply GRCNN in the broader domain of program equivalence. Phrases: program generation, graph-based inputs, flow diagrams, GRCNN, graph recognition convolutional neural network, visual representations, semantic program structures, graph edges, program's structural framework, graph embedding, program-aware, program equivalence, software testing, digital gap, visual structures, semantic structures, program equivalence, test cases, MUX221B, FDT, flow-tables, equivalence, $\Delta$L^2,

This text explores several contraction techniques that have been successfully applied in climate dynamics to derive global climate models with contractive properties. These techniques offer valuable insights into the behavior of climate models, enabling the detection of attractors and assisting in diagnosing climate variability. The methods are presented in detail, along with a demonstration of their application in a simple climate model.

The second generation of kilonovae, which last for a few days after a binary neutron star merger, can be used to measure the properties of the compact objects formed in these events. The light from these objects is often affected by the material ejected in these events, which can provide valuable information through spectroscopy. The reduced opacity of the ejected material allows for the expansion to be measured and gives constraints on the properties of the formed objects. In this study, we corrected an error in previous work and obtained the correct radiative rates for a specific type of electron transition in osmium. We then used this information to calculate the opacities of the material ejected in kilonovae and found that the reduced opacity of these events is directly related to the opacities of osmium and gold. The reduced opacity of these events is directly related to the fill factor of the material ejected and the specific mass of the material ejected. Based on this study, it is possible to measure the properties of the compact objects formed in these events through the reduced opacity of these events. The reduced opacity of these events can be used to distinguish between different types of r-process nucleosynthesis and can be used to test the different types of r-process nucleosynthesis by comparing the reduced opacity of these events to the abundance of these elements in the material ejected in these events.

A breakthrough in medical imaging has been achieved through the advancement of deep learning, enabling the creation of automated segmentation software for the gastrointestinal tract. This innovative technology leverages artificial intelligence to produce precise and human-like image segmentation results, streamlining a complex process previously reliant on time-consuming and labor-intensive manual techniques. Although gastrointestinal disorders are prevalent and necessitate detailed, precise analysis from both radiologists and endoscopists to inform treatment and diagnosis, the traditional manual imaging process has been a barrier to delivering timely and efficient care. The application of deep learning segmentation, as shown in our study using a UNet-based model, has the potential to significantly improve clinical workflows for upper and lower endoscopy procedures, ultimately enhancing patient treatment and diagnosis outcomes.

Given a data set comprised of multiple sample compositions, each composed of the same quantities of components, we can learn about their relationships by calculating various composite values. Commonly used composite metrics include the antilogarithm of the sum of the logarithms (ACV1) and the ratio of the maximum to the minimum component values (R4). By applying multivariate analysis, we can discover and interpret compositional data patterns, particularly those influenced by regional geology or statistical analysis errors. However, direct calculation methods are necessary to calculate the eigenvectors of a square matrix, particularly the principal axes of a positive definite matrix. Furthermore, we can establish lower and upper bounds for the eigenvectors of a matrix with constraints, specifically the eigenvectors of a positive semi-definite matrix with elements that represent a data sample's compositional analysis.

The core/shell model for super-Earths suggests that planet evolution is influenced by abundance and metal enrichment, which are reflected in the planetary mass and radius ratios. This has led to the concept of a 'desert' - the absence of low-mass planets with masses less than about 2 Earth masses and radii less than about 3 times that of Earth, particularly for super-Jupiter planets. However, this idea applies primarily to planets orbiting within the habitable zone of their stars. In this study, we analyzed a sample of 107 planets discovered by CORALIE/HARPS that have been previously published in the Exoplanet European Southern Observatory (ESO) catalogue. We found that there is no deserts at low masses for super-Earths or Sub-Saturn mass planets in our sample and this lack of a desert could be attributed to several biases in the ExoSOAR catalogue, particularly the selection of planets with more massive parent stars and those with orbital periods easier to measure. We found that the Schmitt and Kinman (2016) recipe for calculating surface gravity, which is based on host star mass and radius, is effective in characterizing Sub-Saturn mass planets in our sample. However, this may be a consequence of the selection effects in the ExoSOAR catalogue.

The complex nature of real-world images necessitates the attention of multiple objects, not just one. Current studies in visual tasks like image captioning and visual question answering often concentrate on utilizing the primary object reference. This paper argues that superior performance requires a more comprehensive approach. To this end, we introduce a novel attention regulation technique called Mutual Knowledge Enhancement (MKE) for the multi-object attention mechanism. MKE ensures that all relevant objects are acknowledged by simulating a mutual learning process between network modules, thereby boosting the performance of existing models. Our proposed MKE technique has been successfully applied to the image captioning task and has achieved notable results, surpassing the state-of-the-art performance on the COCO dataset.

To explore the possibility of dark matter composed of two compressed particles,
we analyze a two-component system where each component is made up of a single type of particle.
These particles interact with each other through a Yukawa force and also experience a short-range force
that arises due to their compressed nature and finite size.
As a result, their equilibrium density varies in proportion to $\mu^{-6}$, where $\mu$ is the reduced mass of the particles.
Furthermore, the high compressibility of dark matter allows for a wide range of pressures, which in turn
depends on the characteristics of the particles and their molecular size.
By investigating various values of the Yukawa coupling and pressure of dark matter,
we have found that even weakly-interacting particles can be dense enough to account for dark matter in the universe.
Consequently, the short-range force induced by the compressed nature of dark matter plays a crucial role in determining the density of this type of matter.
Given that the characteristics of the compressed dark matter are different from those of the standard weakly-interacting massive particles,
future research can focus on detecting this type of matter by observing the effects of its non-Yukawa interaction on the structure of the galaxy cluster and its surrounding environment.

Our objective was to see how far the basic recurrent neural network could be taken in its capabilities to perform a range of cognitive tasks, and we achieved this by using a simplified annotation scheme that reflected the actual connections in the brain better than the standard approach. We successfully applied this simplified annotation to various fundamental cognitive tasks including counting, categorization, and prediction through association. The resulting network was able to learn these capabilities significantly faster than the standard method. Furthermore, we observed that the simplified annotation led to more realistic and sparse weight connections being learned by the network, which in turn resulted in improved robustness and performance in the tasks. We also found that the simplified annotation resulted in the creation of internal states that resembled key brain regions' responses to stimuli, which highlights the annotation's biological relevance.

We introduce a method to classify nilpotent algebras based on their geometric properties in low dimensions, which also generates an intrinsic invariance system. By studying this system, we develop an algorithm to categorize nilpotent algebras in all finite dimensions, expressing the invariance in a combinatorial form related to the algebra's linear structure. The resulting classification reveals unique geometric characteristics for each category, enabling the distillation of the invariance into essential linear constraints, thus resolving an unresolved problem from algebra theory.

It's hypothized that supermassive black holes gain mass primarily through the consumption of gas in their environments, becoming active galactic nuclei when the gas within their accretion discs reaches critical velocities and produces luminous jets. High-speed jets emanating from black holes can either terminate abruptly or maintain their velocity by expanding into surrounding intergalactic medium, depending on the mass of the black hole. Recent discoveries by the Edge-Enhanced Delta Function model, which aligns observations with the cosmic microwave background's effect on large-scale structures, reveal that supermassive black holes at the highest redshift existed in environments that were significantly affected by the CMB anisotropy. In this study, we utilize hydrodynamic simulations to explore how the CMB impacts the behavior of these high-redshift black holes and their jets. Our simulation indicates that the CMB causes a slight decrease in the velocity of these high-redshift black holes. Furthermore, the CMB leads to a slight increase in the radius of the region within the accretion disc that the black hole can access, resulting in enhanced fueling but decreased efficiency in energy production from the discs. Conversely, the CMB's influence on high-redshift black holes may lead to decreased fueling of less massive black holes due to increased disc mass, potentially counteracting the CMB's previous predicted effect on AGN prevalence in the universe.

We've discovered that the gravitational field in classical General Relativity can be described by a complex-valued density on spacetime, referred to as a Lagrangian. When the imaginary component of this density is zero, it corresponds to the geometric phase initially proposed by Einstein. Our analysis indicates that multiple geometries can coexist and vary over time. Conversely, under the condition that the Lagrangian's real component remains non-zero, the imaginary component vanishes, and the theory reduces to Einstein's General Relativity. By incorporating a variable mass term into the Lagrangian, we show that gravitational fields can possess internal degrees of freedom. Furthermore, our findings suggest that classical gravity exhibits a self-repulsive characteristic at extremely close distances and a divergent metric at infinitely close distances. Finally, we explore the implications of our results on the underlying structure of spacetime and the nature of gravity itself.

This study presents advancements to the 3D Shift Invariant Feature and corresponding matching algorithm, also incorporating SP-Symmetry for constructing image representations. A method for generating local templates from a model's volume is outlined, leveraging the robust features derived from 3D SIFT. An efficient scheme for grouping these features into a single representative, preserving spatial relationships, is proposed. Furthermore, we demonstrate the compatibility of these features with symmetry properties, enabling the extension of matching procedures to symmetrical image pairs via registration. This approach is evaluated using various datasets, including synthetic and real-world scans, with the added option to automatically determine the most suitable symmetry for a particular volume. Extensive experiments compare our method to state-of-the-art image registration techniques, revealing superior performance in a range of scenarios.

We conducted a comprehensive study of the double-degenerate binary system SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, specifically focusing on its unique 40.5-minute eclipsing binary phenomenon. Through our serendipitous detection of a longer shadow period, double-sided eclipses, and complex light fluctuations, we gained a deeper understanding of this binary's behavior and properties. After generating detailed light curves from our long-term photometry data, we observed the primary eclipses occurring virtually simultaneously for both components, allowing the system's intrinsic orbital period to be determined as 40.477 minutes. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the system's light fluctuations are dominated by non-primary periodic patterns associated with oscillations of the degenerate stars, evident in our individual bandpass light curves as well as a comprehensive fastfold plot. Through our examination of the fastfold plot, we were able to identify a range of oscillation periods spanning from under one minute to over ten minutes. Additionally, our investigation of the system's fastfold plot revealed the presence of significant harmonic content in the system's light fluctuations at multiples of the orbital period and their first few harmonics.

This study reevaluates global image aggregation techniques in light of optimality in transport theory, revealing novel approaches to aggregation that are sensitive to image details and requiring minimal prior knowledge. It also identifies distinct biases inherent in commonly used aggregation operators, such as mean aggregation, which can be corrected by leveraging prior information. Prior knowledge is incorporated into the cost function in the optimality framework. Assuming optimality is achieved through a unique optimal transport plan allows us to derive prior-knowledge-free aggregation operators that are unique up to permutation ambiguity. To accommodate multiple priors, we develop a consensus-based framework, which remains applicable even in the absence of prior knowledge, resulting in operators that are inconsistent without priors. Nonetheless, our findings suggest prior-knowledge-free aggregation operators should be utilized cautiously.

The growing evidence suggests that the properties of a active galactic nucleus' (AGN) surrounding environment significantly influence its beam orientation. By conducting an in-depth study of a sample of radio-selected AGNs, researchers have discovered distinct patterns in the distribution of certain galactic features and radio vector positions. Furthermore, an analysis of the host galaxy morphology reveals significant differences between AGNs of various sub-classes, such as those that are Compton-thick, have certain X-ray characteristics, or fall within specific optical classification categories. Additionally, there are notable variations in the distribution of galaxy features and radio vector positions between the unobscured and obscured AGNs. To further understand these findings, researchers have developed a framework to investigate the potential effects of orientation and the characteristics of the AGN's surrounding environment on radio vector position.

This research paper examines 2-dimensional surfaces within the 4-dimensional Euclidean space. We focus on investigating these surfaces, which by definition, have zero mean curvature. Our key findings reveal that when these surfaces maintain a consistent distance from a fixed point in the Euclidean space, they adhere to spherical symmetry. Additionally, when they do not maintain this consistent distance, we identify two distinct cases: one results in flat surfaces and the other yields positively curved surfaces.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation begins with vast amount of
unlabeled data encrypted in the form of images. Numerous studies have shown that
deep neural networks trained on unlabeled data through self-supervised learning
exhibit superior unlabeled performance compared to supervised learning.
Monocular depth estimation has been shown to be an effective self-supervised
pre-training method for semantic segmentation in various studies. This research
investigates the underlying explanation for this superiority by comparing depth
estimation with classification as self-supervised pre-training methods. An
experimental analysis has been conducted on the SBDv2 and Camille datasets,
revealing that the superiority of depth estimation is mainly attributed to the
overlapping region between two datasets in the course of pre-training. Once the
two datasets are chosen distinctly, classification can serve as a more suitable
self-supervised pre-training method compared to depth estimation.

We introduce TCube, a neural time-series storytelling approach that generates
engaging, chronological narratives from time-series data, encompassing both
technical and business topics. The stories typically comprise an introduction,
followed by a discussion of positives, negatives, and trends, concluding with a
summary. TCube leverages a combination of domain-agnostic and specialized
knowledge to produce high-quality narratives. The method includes: 
- A training pipeline based on GPT-2, allowing it to learn story generation
  automatically;
- A suite of pre-built story templates to accommodate various domains and
  increase generalization;
- An innovative trend detection feature, employing both statistical and
  connectionist methods to identify emerging trends in time-series data;
- A novel trend template, enhancing GPT-2's capabilities to incorporate trend
  information within story generation. 
Experiments reveal that TCube produces stories with trends and positions
  comparable to those of expert-generated content, scored better than a strong
  existing baseline in fluency and coherence, and demonstrated robustness to
  variations in field and data lengths. The code and data can be accessed at
  https://github.com/asharakeh/TCube.

The ATLAS experiment has made a variety of measurements in uncommon beauty meson decays, including those that involve CP violation. This record details the analysis methods, evaluation procedures, and the findings of these measurements.

On a Cayley tree, we explore periodic Ising distributions by considering the smallest period possible, given that local factors in the energy function have a particular structure. Under these conditions, we establish the existence of novel periodic distributions that aren't linked to the traditional symmetry in the system, thus extending existing Clusel-Orlandi and van den Berg-Kesten results. Furthermore, we show that certain periodic characteristics can be exhibited by clusters at any given time.

This research explores the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a broad class of first-order nonlinear hyperbolic partial differential equations, featuring non-strictly hyperbolic conservation laws, with coefficients that decrease at a rate of p(x)/2 < 1/2, in space dimension one and higher, for initial conditions in various function spaces within the context of Lp norms. It is demonstrated that for locally smooth solutions, the coefficients' non-local growth rate has no impact on maintaining the equation's hyperbolic nature, whereas for less smooth solutions, this result indicates an optimal non-local growth restriction for maintaining solution distinctiveness. Moreover, a comprehensive discussion on the non-locality of solutions is provided.

This research introduces Enhanced N-gram Memory Module (ENMM), an improved model for Japanese term segmentation, to address the difficulties posed by highly variable character combinations in the language. The new module is based on the concept of N-gram Memory Module (NMM) commonly used in Chinese character modeling, but with several key modifications. Firstly, the treatment of FURIGANA characters has been optimized, as well as the handling of highly flexible character combinations. The new module essentially employs an augmented n-gram database for prediction purposes. Experiments have been conducted using a specially created dataset for evaluating Japanese term segmentation capacity. The results have demonstrated more efficient use of historical information and higher accuracy rates for term segmentation compared to the standard NMM model.

Software developers on Stack Overflow, a prominent Q&A platform, collaborate with 9968 external organizations, showcasing the significant role these external connections play in facilitating knowledge sharing. This study aimed to uncover the common characteristics of these external collaborations by analyzing user behavior, and how these connections are utilized to address on-topic questions related to software development. The research begins with an analysis of how these external connections are shared, and which users are most active in sharing them. Further investigation compares the topics associated with these external connections to understand their relevance. Moreover, the study examines how these external connections are referenced in questions and answers, and what benefits developers find useful when collaborating with these organizations. Ultimately, the research identifies specific characteristics of successful knowledge-sharing external connections, offering insights that can enhance software development knowledge management and the design of collaborative tools.

The emergence of star-forming galaxies at early cosmological times poses a question about their extinguished activity in the quasilinear regime (~1<=z<=3). We evaluate three theories which attempt to explain this phenomenon: a halt in mass accretion, increased active galactic nucleus feedback, and the internal loss of angular momentum. According to a widely accepted model, each of these factors increases independently with the galaxy's mass. However, this distinction is evaluated in relation to observed data which indicates a correlation between mass and feedback but also an absence of activity in low-mass galaxies despite sufficient accretion and angular momentum for a potential quasar phase. Consequently, it is proposed that feedback might be the primary reason for the suppressed activity in the majority of galaxies. Moreover, it is suggested that mass accretion and angular momentum loss contribute to the diminished luminosity relative to a quasar phase. Numerical simulations which assume a linear correlation between mass and feedback may actually overestimate the efficacy of this feedback, thus masking the potential for further feedback mechanisms. Therefore, it is necessary to conduct more intricate studies taking into account the complex structures and diversity of galaxies.

Establishing and maintaining a critical mass of climate supporters is crucial for motivating society to transition to renewable energy, meet carbon reduction targets, and mitigate global warming. Effective climate communication is necessary to engage the public and achieve societal change, typically involving climate change's severe consequences, such as increased extreme weather events, to persuade others. Since most people are not climate scientists, gaining accurate knowledge about the field and developing strategies to convey that knowledge to others is vital for becoming a successful climate communicator. Our research aims to address this by creating the Climate Information Repository (CIR), an extensive knowledge base containing diverse climate resources, and introducing ClimateAbode, a text generator that combines CIR information to empower impactful climate communication. Experimental results demonstrate the validity of our approach and its potential applications in boosting climate conversations during in-person encounters and online interactions.

The medical field heavily relies on private documents, such as discharge summaries, which contain vital information about patients' signs, such as blood test results, cultures, and radiology reports. Extracting significant event data from these documents is essential for comprehensive patient care, but the availability of annotated data is severely limited due to the high cost of manual labeling. This research addresses the issue of limited data availability by tackling the problem of generalizing sign event extraction across different hospitals and domains using few-shot learning techniques. We propose an end-to-end framework that learns to extract information from unseen domains using data from multiple source domains, demonstrating improved performance on the MedNotes dataset compared to traditional approaches that utilize target-domain samples during training.

The implementation of Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) has been under development for decades due to its potential to improve traffic flow parameters, but widespread implementation has been hindered by the technical challenges involved. Automotive industry leaders perceive a high level of difficulty in deploying ITS technology, primarily because of the diverse environments in which vehicles operate. In this context, Reinforcement Learning has emerged as a promising framework for developing adjustable and effective strategies for vehicles within the framework of an Intelligent Transport System. A comprehensive study illustrates the utilization of Reinforcement Learning in an ITS environment, followed by a comparison of various Deep Reinforcement Learning methods in an experimental setting. This research documents the technical aspects of implementing an ITS and evaluates the performance of DRL-based systems, which can serve as reference points for practitioners in the automotive sector.

This paper presents an improved method for categorizing data in the field of Information Technology with a focus on spiking neural networks, which are highly energy-efficient. The initial concept introduced a novel learning technique known as Back-Propogation Through time, which bypasses the requirement for repeated time-steps in traditional BP algorithms. However, the initial implementation had limitations, which are addressed in this revised version. The improved method yields greater accuracy and reduces energy consumption by 34% compared to the initial implementation. Furthermore, it enables the deployment of large-scale neural networks on smaller FPGAs, which was previously impossible due to power constraints. The computational overhead is increased by approximately 50%.

This research investigates the composition of spin-aligned quark stars at elevated temperatures under the influence of strong magnetic fields. We have computed the free energy, pressure, and entropy associated with radiated photons in the magnetic vacuum. Furthermore, we have determined the equation of state for both strange quark matter and the star in various phases. Utilizing the generalized Bag model, we have derived equations for the mass radius, thermal radius, gravitational binding energy, and thermal energy of the quark star against central density. Our findings demonstrate that the star's mass is directly proportional to the magnetic field strength, with the thermal energy also showing a positive correlation as well.

Current Vue.js web applications can leverage the browser's computational power, utilizing parallel JavaScript execution, to enhance performance. We introduce Pando, a lightweight framework empowering developers to tap into the collective computing power of individual volunteers' browsers. Pando facilitates creators in expanding the scale of their applications by exploiting extra browser resources, effectively tapping into the vast resources offered through the Decentralized Volunteer Computing project. Pando achieves this by implementing innovative techniques, including dynamic JavaScript extension, synchronized data sharing, and synchronized work distribution through a centralized portal, thereby allowing developers to write scalable applications exploiting both local and remote resources seamlessly.

This research presents a new nonparametric method for estimating nonlinear eigenvalues and eigenvectors in a dynamic framework. We apply a nonparametric approach with a specific interpolation scheme to estimate the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a transition matrix. Our estimation method utilizes a two-part formulation: first, estimating nonlinear eigenvalues and deriving the eigenvector projections, and second, estimating eigenvectors while satisfying the eigenvector projection constraint. We demonstrate that our estimators converge at a rate of n^(-2d/(4+2)) under certain conditions, where d represents the dimensionality of the data and n is the number of observations. Furthermore, we substantiate the consistency of our estimators through theoretical analysis. Additionally, we provide simulations and real-world applications, including the analysis of Twitter data and stock price correlations, to showcase the practical utility of our estimators.

In the framework of nuclear dynamics, the process of nucleus-breaking can be understood by analyzing how a fragile system evolves when it loses energy. Researchers have found that in many instances, the transition from a stable nucleus to a non-existent one involves a series of temporary occurrences of nuclei that have not been stable since they have not existed before, which follows the rule that the more energy lost, the more particles are formed and the more stable the nucleus becomes. However, it's been observed that during this energy-loss process, the intensity of the formed non-stable nuclei reaches a maximum at a certain energy loss and then decreases as the system continues to lose energy. This phenomenon occurs because the formation of non-stable nuclei is a local process; as the system approaches the maximum intensity, the non-stable nuclei are so different from the initial nucleus that the local process cannot proceed efficiently. When the system surpasses this intensity, the non-stable nuclei become so similar to the final nucleus that the local process cannot operate either, which causes the intensity of the non-stable nuclei to decrease. This view of nucleus-breaking has been successfully applied to the decomposition of the high-spin high-orientation excitations in even-even nuclei and the dripping-fountain phenomenon. It's been proposed that this view can also be applied to the phenomenon of intermediate beta-transitions by considering the formation of nuclei during the transition process as a series of temporary occurrences of nuclei that have not existed before, which can explain the transfer of strength in the nuclear

This statement introduces the general concept of an $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theory, which serves as a foundation for an innovative approach to understanding how confinement and the breaking of chiral symmetry work in a specific $SU(N_{c})$ gauge theory, particularly when coupled to an $NF$-component vector quark with a unique charge under the chiral $U(N_{F})$ symmetry. The confinement and chiral symmetry breaking transitions in this theory can be identified by analyzing the behavior of the two-point function of a vector quark in both the confining and chiral symmetry breaking phases. This analysis reveals that the same features characteristic of the confining phase in a $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theory as observed in a previous study on a $SU(N_{c})$ gauge theory. Consequently, the findings in this context are equally applicable to both a confining and chiral symmetry breaking environment.

Machine learning models like random forests are widely used due to their ability to accurately predict outcomes across a range of scenarios, yet the processes behind their predictions are often difficult to understand. By breaking down a forest into individual tree decisions and analyzing the relationships between predictor variables at different stages, researchers can identify patterns in data, enhancing the model's interpretability. A new approach, Disentangled Assignment Curves, provides a detailed look at how predictions unfold across multiple trees, revealing insights such as variable importance and non-linear relationships between variables. This method has been successfully tested on datasets with established patterns and real-world data, revealing new insights about patient risk profiles in medical data.

Private neural network training has proven to be a lucrative area of research, and our work at Google focused on addressing model training's data parallelization challenges. We developed Flatee, a framework that utilizes secure multi-party computation and homogeneous multi-server regression to reengineer the training process for large-scale models. By integrating secure computation and TEEs, Flatee provides enterprises with a reliable solution for collaborative machine learning across multiple organizations. Our platform allows companies to train neural networks using their own confidential data, even when working together and relying on different hardware for their systems. We have successfully trained several notable models, including MobileNetV2 and ResNet-50, using the TensorFlow framework. We found our approach to provide significant improvements in training efficiency, and our results remain efficient and fast. We are eager to share Flatee with the research community to further drive innovation in this field.

A new automated method for evaluating the capabilities of robotic systems has been developed, which involves assessing their performance in high-level tasks without manual intervention. The proposed automation feature can be incorporated into the pipeline for detecting and tracking objects across various distances and environments. The integration of this tool enables improved object handling tasks via a robotic system consisting of a compact vision system and a tracking device. By including this capability, the detection and identification of objects can be enhanced, particularly in situations where the camera has a limited field of view.

This paper introduces a novel approach to automate the creation of security policies for containerized microservices by generating security checks from security configurations. When deploying secure microservices in containers, administrators typically specify security policies, but these policies are often bypassed or disregarded, either intentionally or unintentionally, through various security threats. To address this issue, we propose the Timeloops method, which learns security controls for microservices by generating security checks based on security configurations, thus enabling the creation of secure microservices deployments. By integrating Timeloops with a fault-tolerant testing framework, we validate its effectiveness and efficiency in generating security controls for microservices. Furthermore, we examined the performance of Timeloops in handling various security scenarios and compared its efficiency to manual security provisioning approaches.

Real-world datasets often comprise items with interdependent aspects, where reduction to basic attributes fails to capture context-specific relationships among aspects. To address this shortcoming, a method called Linear Classifiers in Item Space Shapes aims to leverage datasets in their original complexity to classify individual item aspects. The approach involves representing items as multidimensional geometrical entities with intrinsic properties and interaspect connections. Theoretical analysis and experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world data sets demonstrate that this method achieves higher accuracy compared to standard attribute-based classifiers, especially in cases where items exhibit geometric relationships to each other.

We studied the orbital distribution of massive stars within four large galaxies, applying detailed stellar spectroscopy and structural analysis. By utilizing the stellar velocities in conjunction with a robust method for calculating the galaxy's central black hole spin, we re-examined the stellar arrangement around the black hole in these galaxies. Unlike previous findings, we discovered a distinct pattern of mass annuli that didn't always correlate with population segregation. However, when we focused on the stellar populations near the black hole, we observed clear separation and preferential alignment of stars based on population type. Furthermore, we found that population segregation is more pronounced when considering narrow mass ranges close to the black hole. Using custom-built Monte Carlo simulations, we identified demographic changes in the stellar populations within a 1 kpc radius around the black hole and found that a significant increase in high-mass stars appears to accompany the transition from a quiescent phase to an active phase. By comparing our results to theoretical models, we observed agreement with the predicted effects of a bar structure on stellar arrangement, particularly in terms of population segregation in the central black hole region.

We demonstrate an instance of random model predictive regulation working in a simulated 10-state system affected by random disturbances. Despite insignificant knowledge of the disturbance, we show that RMPC can successfully operate without reference to an optimal disturbance reduction strategy, merely using a basic linear control policy, thereby maintaining the system within specified limits. Moreover, the method's probabilistic nature enables us to analyze and confirm the likelihood of system state convergence and disturbance reduction within designated bounds. The case study highlights that, in the absence of an optimal disturbance reduction strategy, RMPC can function with a deeper level of certainty and maintain system safety constraints when dealing with uncertain disturbances.

Deep learning's continuous innovation and rising adoption have led to growing autonomy needs in large-scale deep model training. Developing large models incurs significant computational and storage costs, while the extensive data required for effective training poses significant data preparation challenges. Certain applications can't meet these costs due to resource constraints or data availability issues. These cost and efficiency gaps can't be ignored in real-world scenarios. Our research focuses on understanding the underlying principles of autonomous component analysis and exploring the associated technical problems. We start by explaining the core concept of autonomous component analysis and its essential ingredients. We then examine the critical issue of dictionary learning, which is central to this approach. We delve into the related tasks of sparse representation and dictionary refinement. Comprehensive numerical experiments are conducted to illustrate the effectiveness of this method in various practical contexts.

A new species model is developed based on a chaotic version of the voter model. This model, which involves a two-species competition in a random environment, is shown to have a novel connection to the nutrient-limited growth of single-culture populations in ecology. By integrating the species' population dynamics with random movements, a species' extinction process is demonstrated through a crossover between voter-like dynamics on the surface of a sphere and the Bak-Tang- Wang model. The combined effects of random movements and competitive interactions can either lead to a species' total extinction, a mutually exclusive relationship, or ecologically stable coexistence. The species' extinction probability is found to be dependent on the magnitude of random movements and the complexity of its environment. The model is supported by numerical simulations, which also reveal a diverse array of ecologically relevant patterns, including wave patterns, chaotic behavior, and the formation of distinct species regions.

In the context of the abelian quantum dual model, regions of a lattice represent quantum operators, with corresponding von Neumann algebras formed by combinations of these operators. By studying how these region algebras interact, researchers can gain insights into the holographic properties of the model. Our analysis focuses on a specific collection of algebras corresponding to larger and larger collections of connected regions. We demonstrate that this network of algebras has a cohesive structure, in which any given algebra is part of a comprehensive whole, and establish that it comprises an increasing sequence of algebras representing the entire space. Additionally, our results show that interface reflection symmetries exist within the model, and that the relationship between a region's shape and its algebra is inherent.

A theoretical model for magnomechanics in three-dimensional chambers is developed, incorporating the classical influence of a feedback circuit on magnons and phonons. It is discovered that in this entanglement-enhancing system, increasing the intensity of the feedback laser or decreasing the phonon decay rate leads to improved tripartite entanglement. The optimal combination of these parameters enables the generation of highly stable, symmetric dark modes which amplify entanglement. This concept is expected to contribute to the research of complex spin-mechanical systems and related quantum simulations.

We've developed a comprehensive collection of one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for both space- and time-regulated QCD, displaying the full dependence on dimensional parameters in the latter case. This collection is based on a previous single-scale analysis, with the added benefit of being independent of any scale. While the space-regulated result is a revision of an existing work, the time-regulated result is an original contribution. Additionally, we've found that while double-collinear splitting operators are unaffected by dimensional parameters, their enforcement leads to the cancellation of typically non-zero soft terms, potentially hindering double-soft corrections. This cancellation likely extends to soft interactions beyond the triple-collinear context, suggesting the need for a differential form of the dimensional regularization parameter to accurately represent double-soft effects.

A formal proof for the Neron Desingularization, a multidimensional case algorithm, has been formulated and applied to one-dimensional local domains, and this concept is currently being used within Singular software implementation. Furthermore, a relevant theorem based on Greenberg's Strong Infiniteness Theorem has also been introduced and applied to the construction of a multidimensional, generalized Neron Desingularization for one-dimensional local domains.

Ancient sundials held significant cultural importance in interpreting time across diverse civilizations. As the primary time-telling device before the widespread use of mechanical clocks, sundials also played a crucial role in Indonesian daily life, particularly during the Islamic Golden Age. With the advent of mechanical clocks, their usage gradually declined and they were eventually forgotten. To document their remaining examples, a 2019 project titled Suryakala-Nusantara was launched. Combining geographic information systems and photogrammetry, the project aimed to create detailed spatial models and high-resolution images of sundials. After collecting data from 211 districts across 33 provinces, the project resulted in the collection and analysis of 304 sundials. To raise awareness about the historical significance of sundials through community engagement and education, a series of workshops and conferences were held, featuring presentations on the project's findings to local communities, students, and academics. As a legacy, an online platform and mobile application were developed to showcase the documented sundials and explain their cultural importance. With the success of Suryakala-Nusantara, similar projects are now being replicated in other countries.

This research introduces a new concept called integrated data and power networking coexisting D2D communications. A reflective surface with intelligence is placed in a device-to-device (D2D) network to reflect signals for two users, enhancing their data rate and energy efficiency by optimizing a joint reflection matrix and transmit power vector. A series of efficient algorithms have been developed to tackle this optimization problem, including a convex-concave alternating projection algorithm, a distributed algorithm using a successively regularized dual approach, and a near-optimal and distributed algorithm employing successive convex approximation. Numerical results demonstrate the efficacy of these algorithms in achieving high data rates and power efficiency for D2D communications.

The use of LDV in studying complex flows has been significantly impacted by the ability to obtain precise two-dimensional data quickly and efficiently. This capability allows researchers to gain valuable insights into intricate fluid interactions, even when the associated fringe pattern quality remains suboptimal. By leveraging the fine-scale details captured in the LDV measurements, researchers can determine the nature of flow phenomena in intricate systems, such as highly turbulent flows, composite flows, and fluid dynamics associated with airfoil surfaces. This review will focus on the development and implementation of an advanced LDV system designed to obtain sharp 2D data from a single-point measurement technique. We will examine the benefits and limitations of this system and highlight its potential applications in complex flow research.

In the commentary, an in-depth analysis is provided for an abstract framework outlining possible uncountable orders for first-order spectra of binary relation structures, with a proof supplement demonstrating that these orders are indeed feasible for first-order binary relation theories.

The effectiveness of a programmable phase disk was assessed in this research as a solution to correct for aberrations in a Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM). The study utilized a computationally generated phase mask to test this approach. The findings show that the phase mask's phase depth needs to be substantially increased for it to be utilized directly in an TEM system without an imaging lens. However, this constraint can be overcome by feeding the lens's parameters and the desired phase mask into an algorithm that calculates the required lens adjustments to achieve the desired phase mask. The study successfully applied this method to correct both linear and nonlinear aberrations. The phase mask was also utilized to correct spherical aberration in an in-situ imaging experiment. The study's results provide foundational guidance for the integration of programmable phase masks into TEM systems to facilitate corrected phase imaging.

In the context of assessment, calculators are indispensable tools, enabling
students to concentrate on computational challenges rather than struggling
with mechanical calculations that can hinder their ability to think. As the
stakeholders in assessment, we must decide whether specific calculators are
essential for understanding graphical and numerical concepts. This study
provides a method for determining the required calculator functions by
identifying the essential calculations for each concept. By breaking down each
concept into necessary computations, we can determine the minimal calculator
capabilities needed for comprehension. This process not only determines which
calculators are necessary but also serves as a resource for developing those
calculators and testing their functionality.

Consider a lattice point movement in the positive orthant of a d-dimensional integer space. To attain a specific location, we calculate the number of unique paths using unit-step movements, summing the steps in the same direction. For achieving a location with k steps in one dimension, there are $(k+1)(k+2)/2$ possible paths. A closed-form expression is derived for determining the number of paths, denoted as $P_{d,K}(m)$, to reach a multidimensional location $m = (m_1, \dots, m_d)$ in the positive orthant of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, where each dimension $i$ has $K_i$ steps. The obtained expression is used to compute the volume of the lattice sphere with radius $r$ in this context, resulting in $\sum_{m_1=m_2=\dots=m_d=0}^r P_{d,K(r)}(m) $, where $K(r)$ is the maximum step count across all dimensions. For small d and large r, this volume approximates the volume of the standard sphere in $L_2$-norm.

By applying the GOP model to black hole spacetimes, the dimensionally expanded metric can be developed and used to calculate quasinormal frequencies. This approach yields a viable method for determining the parameters of unknown black holes. Taking the case of a $D$-dimensional polymerized Schwarzschild black hole as a test object, we derived formulas for quasinormal frequencies of both tensor and scalar perturbations in the approximation limit. Furthermore, we calculated and tabulated quasinormal frequencies in various dimensions and modes. This work offers potential applications in studying the properties of black holes in distinct dimensions and their quasinormal spectra.

In graphene, the Dirac nodes at the Fermi points behave as magnetic monopoles in the Fermi sea's charge landscape. The incorporation of impurities in graphene causes a thermal distortion of the Dirac distribution, resulting in an energy gain known as the particular heat. We demonstrate in our study that this heating effect is accompanied by a decrease in the long-range electromagnetic interaction between distant sites in graphene, which is significant at high temperatures corresponding to the scale of the Dirac quasiparticle's spread. The particular heat is found to be split into two components: one caused by the charge fluctuations associated with the Dirac quasiparticles, and another by the non-local screening of the quasiparticle's magnetic charge. The latter component causes an anomalous, temperature-dependent reduction in the long-range coupling constant. Our analysis assumes the presence of short-range interactions between quasiparticles and treats the graphene panels as thin slabs with electric fields confined to the surfaces.

The masked speech approach has yielded success in speech synthesis, a technique where masked speech is used as input to a text-to-speech model to determine the speaking style and then the speech code is generated from unmasked speech. However, this approach poses a problem as the speaker's identity information is lost during masking.  In this research, a new speaker identification feature is developed which combines both masked and unmasked speech, allowing existing masked speech synthesis architectures to produce high-quality speech with a distinct speaking style.  The proposed method is tested and shown to produce speech with a natural speaking style and the speaker's identity is easily recognizable.  Compared to a model that only uses unmasked speech, the proposed method produces a 90% equivalent quality score and a 95% similarity score for the speaker's identity.

A newly developed statistical framework, called predictive inference, uses machine learning models to generate predictions outside of training data ranges. However, current approaches face challenges when outside data points fall beyond the training distribution. This paper proposes a novel predictive method called Hidden Space Mapping Predictive Inference (HSM-PI), which adapts a well-established machine learning model to tackle this statistical issue. HSM-PI relies on a separate neural network trained in conjunction with the primary model to capture the hidden data dimensions within the training dataset. This mapping is then utilized to determine the most probable data bounds for new, unseen test data. HSM-PI's separation of the hidden data dimensions and mapping processes enables them to learn these characteristics more effectively. Our experiments demonstrate that HSM-PI surpasses existing predictive methods when evaluating out-of-distribution performance. Additionally, HSM-PI achieves superior or comparable results on in-distribution predictive tasks.

Recent breakthroughs in machine learning have led to the widespread adoption of models that can be manipulated by attackers who control the flow of data in a Person-in-the-Middle (PiM) position. Our investigation reveals that machine learning attackers do not necessarily need to possess a sophisticated understanding of the model to successfully launch an attack, as a simple generative model is enough to achieve adverse results. Through our analysis, we demonstrate that PiM attacks can be carried out using a variety of generative models, such as autoregressive and transformer-based models, under the condition that the attacker has a significant advantage in terms of data availability. Our findings also stem from real-world experiments conducted across the gadget and food classification datasets and provide actionable insights for developers on how to enhance the robustness of their models against generative PiM attacks.

Climate change communication is complicated by the proliferation of conspiracy theories, particularly through social media platforms. These platforms serve as a breeding ground for conspiracy theories due to issues like the credibility of source information shared by users. The impact of conspiracy theory dissemination on society is significant, fostering a false narrative and undermining sound climate change discourse. To date, research into social media-based conspiracy theories has focused on evaluating user engagement but neglected to distinguish between various climate change conspiracy theories. To address this gap, our research explores multiple climate change conspiracy theories, including one claiming climate change causes an increase in earthquakes and another stating it leads to temperature fluctuations in the wrong season. We analyzed tweets related to these conspiracy theories, examining which topics they surround and the metrics by which they spread. Interestingly, our findings reveal certain characteristics associated with the dissemination of such conspiracy theories, including user engagement metrics and the involvement of certain users. Crucially, we discovered that promoting conspiracy theories can create a polarized effect among social media users.

Researchers at the CERN LHC have analyzed data from proton-proton collisions, totalling 35.9 inverse femtobarns, and examined single top quark and top quark pair production coupled with unknown particles influencing the events. They discovered that top quark pairs exhibited an excess of events with unaligned transverse momentum relative to the leading jet, and found that the cross-sectional values matched predictions for a singular scalar boson weighing around 750 GeV. No significant differences were found between the observed and predicted angular distributions of the unaligned transverse momentum in events featuring a solitary top quark or a top quark pair. Follow-up searches for pairs of scalar bosons or a singular boson paired with quarks or gluons did not reveal any notable deviations from anticipated results. Given that the cross-sectional value for the singular boson peaks at 750 GeV was found to be 12 femtobarns with a 3.4 femtobarns uncertainty, the possibility that dark matter of 750 GeV is produced in events featuring a solitary top quark or a top quark pair is reduced by approximately 2.7 standard deviations.

Given an n-exangulated framework (C, D, F), we develop a duality theorem analogous to Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality. This duality theorem has as a corollary a duality theorem for n-potent frameworks (C, D, F), as well as a duality theorem for n-potent modules over a finite-dimensional algebra. Additionally, we establish a generalization of the duality theorem for n-potent frameworks to a broader class of frameworks that satisfy a specific angulated reflection property.

Instrumental variables analysis assumes the instrumental variable must always be categorized in a particular order. This paper presents an innovative model that allows for instrumental variables to have various treatment options with no inherent ranking. By applying this model to higher education data in the UK, we find the economic benefits of certain degrees to be distinct from one another.

The interplay of compact stars' strong density and low-temperature conditions creates unique environments that can form various exotic states of matter. Researchers propose an experiment at a high-energy electron beam facility to study these conditions by producing a large number of antineutrons, baryons, and other particles. The experiment involves targeting a narrow energy range near the baryon form factor using an intense, focused electron beam. The predicted number of antineutrons and baryons produced in this experiment is on the order of 10^(-3) to 10^(-2) per second, within a 10^-10 sB-induced background level. The collected data will allow scientists to study antinucleon-nucleon interaction at very low energies, ultimately leading to a deeper understanding of the breaking of discrete symmetries and the composition of the nucleus. Furthermore, the experiment's results will provide valuable insights for future nuclear and particle physics research, particularly for studies involving compact stars and supernova GRAVE. The proposed experiment is expected to be realized using existing or near-term-generation beam facilities. The predicted number of antineutrons and baryons produced in this experiment is on the order of 10^(-3) to 10^(-2) per second, within a 10^-10 sB-induced background level. Hierarchical systems consisting of a triple star system and a disk, with the disk interacting primarily with the outer two stars, experience a balance between gravitational forces and the pressure of the disk's gas particles. This equilibrium is reflected in the disk's structure and the orbital parameters of the stars. Notably, the rates at which the stars in these systems move away from their primary positions vary. Researchers have found that, under the influence of the disk, the outer star in these systems tends to move further away from its initial position more rapidly than the middle star. Conversely, the middle star is often found to be moving further away from its initial position more rapidly than the inner star. This study provides a theoretical explanation for these increasing orbital distances and the associated acceleration disparities among the stars in these systems. The researchers have determined that the discrepancies in these increasing orbital distances are primarily the result of the differences in the stars' initial masses, with higher mass stars experiencing greater increases in their orbital distances. Additionally, the discrepancies in these increasing orbital distances may be influenced by the stars' loss of angular momentum due to interactions with the disk in these systems. The researchers have found that, under the influence of the disk, the outer star in these systems tends to move further away from its initial position more rapidly than the middle star, which in turn is moving further away from its initial position more rapidly than the inner star.

This article examines flat cosmology models based on a lattice theory to describe the universe's theoretical framework. The article discusses the inherent characteristics of these models, specifically the ones based on de Sitter space and Wheeler-DeWitt time, in the context of quantum gravity. The anisotropic, lattice-based models of cosmology are explored, along with their connection to the FRW model. The potential implications of these models for understanding the universe's asymmetries are discussed.

In computer vision, the goal of image segmentation is to divide an image into distinct regions that exhibit homogeneous characteristics. The K-means algorithm is a widely used unsupervised method for image segmentation, which has limitations in its unsophisticated low-level image representation and resulting partitions. To enhance image segmentation, our approach integrates the strengths of state-of-the-art image processing techniques, specifically image denoising and deblurring, into a advanced image representation. We couple these representations with a higher-level image partitioning model to obtain improved segmentation results. The combined influence of higher-level constraints and lower-level image representations enables the differentiation of region boundaries from gradient areas and achieves visually plausible segmentation results. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through numerical evaluations and applications to multiple test datasets.

Active supermassive black holes, which include their accompanying accretion disks, set up a dynamic environment that responds sensitively to the amplification of their surrounding disks due to the effects of superradiance. As a result, any superradiant mode that grows rapidly will eventually be truncated by the constraints of equal spin alignment between the black hole and protons in the disk, assuming the protons reach an equilibrium state through interactions with the surrounding plasma. Our investigations focus primarily on the points of peak growth occurring in the superradiant spectrum, specifically for the $m=0, 1, 2$ modes, and how the associated timeframes of peak growth relate to the mass of the ultralight bosons involved. Additionally, we utilize constraints on massive black hole growth, as well as observations of ultraluminous optical variability, to set lower limits on the boson mass. For instance, for bosons with $1/4\, M_\odot$ mass, variations in the $z\sim 2$ quasars' optical band allow us to establish a lower limit of $\log_{10} (t_{\rm A}/\rm day)\gsim 6.3$. Furthermore, our findings for the $m=0$ mode reveal that the boson mass is further constrained by the observed constraints of massive quasar growth, with the variation factor controlled by a power law that includes the boson mass as its base exponent

Creating hardware with artificial intelligence embedded has several advantages, such as enhanced security and efficiency, although it presents complex challenges like balancing spike propagation and electrical interference. Integrating artificial neural networks onto chipsets requires propagating information efficiently, which is a complex problem to solve. Computational models like the spiking neural network simulator Brian and the brain-inspired chip Loihi can be used to explore this problem. Since Brian and Loihi address neural networks from different perspectives, bridging the two frameworks poses a significant challenge. In this research, we develop an emulator called Brian2Loihi, which enables direct mapping of Brian network parameters to Loihi's architecture, enabling comparison of simulation results between software emulation and hardware implementation. Furthermore, we perform a detailed analysis of network parameters and evaluate network performance under real-world conditions, demonstrating that Brian2Loihi can accurately replicate software simulations in hardware settings.

A solar noise storm is created by intense plasma phenomena on the Sun, typically involving small plasma areas localized in space. The study of these storms provides valuable insights into the processes governing the Sun's atmosphere. Researchers analyzed data from the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA), which allowed them to track the changes in intensity, frequency, and polarization of these storms over time and within different spatial areas. These observations revealed correlations between the characteristics of these storms as they evolve. It was found that during a microflare associated with one of these storms, the polarization of its source component began to vary. This variation led to a change in the frequency, and subsequently, the intensity of the source also changed. These findings indicate that the plasma within these storm sources is dynamic and highly nonlinear, and that the storms' characteristics are interconnected and evolve dynamically.

A discussion on the principles behind an innovative type of optical trap has been presented. Unlike conventional optical traps, which rely on a focused beam, this new design utilizes two planar beams. Research has demonstrated that, under specific conditions, this setup can create a trap with a characteristic shape similar to a doughnut. Furthermore, it has been found that the planar trap offers numerous benefits over conventional methods, including reduced laser power requirements, a larger choice of refractive index ranges, and the ability to control the trap's location more precisely. The advantages of this new type of trap have been highlighted in the context of experiments involving ultra-cold atoms. The feasibility of this new trap concept is likely to be extended to other applications involving particles, such as trapped atoms, ions, and nanoparticles.

The spherically symmetric interaction between a black hole and a vast interstellar cloud, composed of collisionless particles carrying angular momentum, is investigated using the Toomre approximation. This model reveals that a boundary, denoted the Quasi-Static Barrier, emerges due to conservation of angular momentum, effectively limiting the cloud's radius. Only particles with sufficient energy to surpass the Quasi-Static Barrier can directly fall onto the black hole, thereby defining an Accretion Interface. Within this context, we introduce the Accretion Rate, a crucial parameter that helps us analyze how angular momentum affects this process. By comparing the Accretion Rate in the non-rotating and rotating scenarios, we observe that for a non-rotating black hole, the Accretion Rate is determined by the cloud's free-fall time, whereas in the rotating scenario, it is influenced by both the cloud and the Quasi-Static Barrier's properties. Furthermore, we note that for a rotating black hole, the Accretion Rate is sensitive to the ratio of angular momentum support within the Accretion Interface to the total angular momentum received from the stellar sphere. When this ratio approaches 100%, the Accretion Rate diminishes to zero, as the Accretion Interface's properties resemble that of free-fall. By calculating mass-radius relationships for various spin parameters, we gain better understanding of the Quasi-Static Barrier's behavior, particularly as the black hole spin increases.

The rate at which a moving atom emits radiation is highest when its relative velocity to the mirror is optimal, reaching nearly 90% of the maximum emission rate achievable through stationary atoms. Research has found that rapid electromagnetic emissions are caused by the repeated passing of highly oscillating electric fields between the atom and the mirror, leading to a resonance effect. An experiment is proposed to verify this phenomenon by utilizing a scanning mirror and an atom within a molecular ion, demonstrating the potential for a new quantum electrodynamics test.

The extraordinary young cluster Westerlund 2 is home to a stunning collection of over 2000 late-type stars, many of which are engaged in lively binary interactions. A recent study focused on the cluster's outskirts and discovered a significant concentration of red supergiants, spanning multiple degrees of separation from the cluster center. These red supergiants are remarkably young – typically less than 15 million years old – and their presence suggests that the cluster's massive parent cloud continued to feed the cluster's stars for an extended period. This phenomenon is most pronounced at the cluster's outskirts, where the lack of mass has prevented the formation of more massive stars. It is proposed that the cluster's initial mass distribution skewed towards lower mass stars, and as the cluster aged, the distribution shifted towards more massive stars due to a distinct second generation of supernovae and star formation.

This paper introduces a versatile deep learning model that can enhance digitized handwritten documents while maintaining the original text. The network is trained using a large dataset of degraded handwritten documents and demonstrates effective removal of noise, reducing pixel fragmentation, and improving overall legibility. Notably, the model achieves these improvements without altering the existing text, ensuring that the output matches the quality of the input at a pixel-level basis. The developers propose a multi-task adversarial network design to tackle this complex problem, consisting of a feature extraction module for text recognition, a generator producing improved images from degraded ones, and a discriminator verifying the generated image's authenticity. The team leverages a multi-task adversarial loss and two discriminators for text and feature extraction to train the network. The pipeline's end-to-end training allows the network to effectively extract handwritten text features and a domain-specific discriminator is implemented to verify the text's authenticity. The proposed model exhibits superior performance compared to a conventional restoration network, as evidenced by visual comparisons and quantitative evaluations of the generated images. Additionally, the team successfully enhances handwritten text for optical character recognition tasks with notable improvements in character recognition accuracy and reduced error rates.

Indonesia's population growth is substantial, resulting in an escalating need for efficient document processing in the country. To address this need, a reliable and accurate extraction tool is crucial for population and national identity documents.
