This study aims to develop a document extraction tool, specifically designed for Indonesian identity documents (KTP/IKTP), utilizing Image-to-Text (ITT) optical character recognition (OCR) technology and Text-to-SQL Natural Language Processing (NLP) capabilities. To overcome the limitations of conventional ITT/OCR technology and efficiently extract required information, a pre-processed scanning technique is implemented. The developed system is then evaluated using an accumulated dataset of ID card images from various sources. The experimental outcomes indicate that the combination of the proposed scanning technique, NLP, and OCR has yielded superior results, with an extraction accuracy rate of 98% and an overall processing time of 30 seconds per ID card.

In vehicular communications, the IEEE 802.11p standard is widely employed. However, its reliability is hindered by IEEE 802.11p's persistent over-estimation of channel conditions, resulting in unnecessary data re-transmissions. To address this issue, researchers have proposed various short-term and long-term equalization methods for channel analysis. However, these solutions do not take into account the unique characteristics of vehicular networks. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces a Temporal Averaging LSTM (TA-LSTM) driver for channel assessment. The TA-LSTM driver leverages time-averaged weights for adapting to changing channel environments, while also incorporating a control algorithm for optimizing the IEEE 802.11p protocol's legacy functions. The TA-LSTM driver was then integrated into a IEEE 802.11p base station transmitter. The results demonstrate that the TA-LSTM driver achieves optimal performance in reducing re-transmission rates, outperforming legacy IEEE 802.11p and a deep learning model known as deep reinforcement learning.

This research introduces a novel application of Generative Adversarial Networks in colorizing historical black and white celestial images. An image editing technique called tinting was employed to develop a multi-stage training process, which initially creates a database of new colorized images from original pairs and assesses their authenticity. We utilize a content loss calculation to determine the similarity between the original and new images. Additionally, we establish a network that replicates the process of taking black and white photographs to generate new, colorized images based on the original captures. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through a qualitative comparison of the method with another renowned image colorizing technique and an analysis of the benefits and limitations of our proposed model. Furthermore, we successfully applied our method to a collection of historical celestial images.

In 1989, Malliavin demonstrated that any multivariate continuous function can be accurately represented as a finite sum of products between smooth functions and their corresponding partial derivatives. This discovery was inspired by the Universal Approximation Theorem for feedforward neural networks, which was subsequently proven by Hartmann in 1999. Building on this idea, we developed a novel neural network model, referred to as the Malliavin Neural Network (MNN), that incorporates the gradient-free backpropagation framework. The MNN model enables efficient end-to-end training without relying on backpropagation, achieving a speedup of up to 100x compared to the traditional backpropagation method. The MNN model exhibits comparable accuracy to the conventional neural network, according to our experimental findings. Additionally, the MNN model demonstrates resilient performance under adversarial attacks, preserving its effectiveness even when subjected to imperceptible distortions. Furthermore, the MNN model displays a significant decrease in memory requirements without sacrificing accuracy, making it a highly compact model.

This transfer report outlines the accomplishments of the ECFA Early Career Researcher's Committee (ECRCC) from 2021 to 2022. The committee's structure, purpose, and methods are described in detail. The report provides an overview of ECRCC's initiatives and achievements throughout its initial two-year term. The committee's activities fell under three main categories: 1) fostering connections among early career researchers; 2) gathering input from early career researchers and implementing their suggestions; 3) disseminating essential information and offering training. The committee successfully executed multiple online social events, gathered vital feedback from ECFA's early career researchers through a survey, and created educational materials addressing topics of high importance to early career researchers. The report concludes by acknowledging challenges faced by the committee and proposes potential enhancements for future growth.

Research in metastructures has yielded numerous approaches to control waves across various frequency ranges, yet most studies focus on a single type of wave. This work proposes a dual metastructure that can concurrently manipulate both line and point sources to direct wave energy and create multiple isolated bands. Although the concept of dual metastructures was initially introduced for radio frequency applications, our approach adapts it for use in optical frequency ranges due to the ease of fabricating micro- and nano-scale structures. We present a mathematical model describing two types of resonances – a monotonic and an oscillating pattern – that allow for the design of efficient optical tunable meta-materials with novel properties.

Advancements in cooperative learning between humans and robots could significantly expand their potential in various applications, albeit novel transdisciplinary challenges arise from integrating human learning theories into robotic cooperation design. Current cognitive architectures used for robot cooperation often rely on simplified models of human learning, which may not be adapted to handle the complexity of cooperative learning. As a result, cooperative learning systems often fall short in their ability to scale, particularly when dealing with larger systems. Moreover, the cognitive processes employed by existing cooperative learning systems lack transparency, making it difficult to understand how they learn to collaborate. To address these challenges, this paper outlines key requirements for designing cognitive architectures that can facilitate transparent and scalable learning among multiple agents. It also discusses the current state of cognitive architectures in robotics in relation to the specified requirements, followed by a case study illustrating the implementation of transparent and scalable learning mechanisms within a multi-agent system. Through this case study, we demonstrate the ability of cognitive architectures to facilitate transparent and scalable learning among multiple agents.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the average absolute deviation of a normal distribution around its median, with the goal of addressing the challenges in estimating this quantity, which often results in biased estimates when using alternative methods such as the influence functions or banding approaches. By first modifying the bias-corrected estimator of the mean absolute deviation proposed by Donnelly, this study develops an alternative expression which can then be applied in a novel estimator of the average absolute deviation. The proposed estimator demonstrates superiority over existing alternatives through simulations.

This paper focuses on the under-constrained task of identifying relationships. As there are numerous possible connections between two subjects, their associated objects can provide clues about their relationship. We developed and employ a new paradigm of connection prediction, where a model predicts the connection of a given object when paired with a subject from a pre-selected range of domains. Our proposed framework leverages the potential of pre-trained transformers in conjunction with a simple multi-task approach to achieve superior outcomes in both connection prediction and relation discovery tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our model excels at both connection prediction and relation discovery tasks when compared to the baseline models.

The behavior of anisotropic momentum flows in a complex three-dimensional space has been further investigated. We have used the quasi-particle Debye mass formula to determine the disintegration characteristics of quarkonia in a situation of high temperature and finite baryonic chemical potential. The results indicate that anisotropy has a significant impact on the quarkonia's binding characteristics. We have calculated the binding parameters of quarkonia and examined their stability in the presence of anisotropic momentum flows. We have also investigated the disintegration characteristics of quarkonia and obtained the disintegration temperature and width in this context. We have compared our findings with the existing data from other researchers and incorporated them into a complex picture of quarkonia disintegration in a complex environment.

We investigated the low-temperature magnetic arrangements of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7, which exhibit similar  chain structures, within the $R$3$'c$ space group. Unlike other materials with isolated $d^5$ chain magnetism, we found that Tb3RuO7 exhibits partial disordering of its low-temperature rutile-type structure at low temperatures, which is caused by the ratio of intra- and inter-chain interactions. As a result, the $Ru^{4+}$ ions experience an uneven internal magnetic field from $Tb^{3+}$ ions, which leads to two possible states with spin projections of 1 or -1. Furthermore, neutron-diffraction measurements revealed the simultaneous occurrence of antiferromagnetic long-range ordering of $Tb^{3+}$ ions at 4.5 K and the partial disordering of $Ru^{3+}$ ions above 2.5 K in Tb3RuO7. A theoretical model explaining the origin of partial disordering is also presented.

Deep Functional Networks (DFNs) are a type of neural network that was inspired by an analytical method, using generalized linear models, for creating predictive functions. One benefit of DFNs is that they interpret predictions in the context of input features. However, standard training of DFNs assumes a fixed input format, which doesn't accommodate unknown or varying data formats. To address this issue, we've developed a training algorithm for DFNs using a variational autoencoder component to standardize data formats. To improve the generality of feature-based representations in neural networks, we've also developed a new method, using a modulated activation pattern that starts with a basic activation shape. This method allows networks to learn common patterns among input data. Our experiments show that our approach produces accurate predictions and provides interpretable results in the domains of image recognition and molecular property prediction.

Machine learning models are becoming increasingly effective due to advances in data collection and analysis. However, these models can struggle with changes in real-world environments, such as variations in patient demographics in medical settings. Our proposed solution involves the semi-generative modeling approach, which utilizes information from expert knowledge and current data to adapt to real-world conditions. Our method draws on the principles of causal inference, enabling the identification of underlying patterns despite noisy data correlations. Our research demonstrates that semi-generative models like Copula NR can effectively handle instances of covariate shift and outperform traditional generative modeling techniques. Furthermore, the Copula NR model exhibits desirable qualities such as data protection capabilities and the ability to streamline large data sets while maintaining accurate representations of the original data distribution.

In this overview, we'll explore how deep learning works by examining its geometric properties. By considering the inherent structure of deep neural networks, we can gain insights into their behavior, which will ultimately guide the development of more efficient training methods.

Jorgensen introduced the concept of a minimal set of elements $S$ in a lattice $L$ where $x \in L$, $x \neq 0$, and for every $s \in S$, the least prime division of $x$ relative to $s$ exists. We research lattices satisfying a specific condition based on this definition, leading to a discovery about heights within these lattices, and also find heights to be equal to lattice depths in a particular case. Additionally, we identify a particular example of a lattice satisfying the given condition while possessing sublattices of a specific order.

Machine learning (ML) technologies power an array of cutting-edge applications, such as cutting-edge physics research, however, difficulties arise when users depend on black-box algorithms due to the lack of transparent decision-making processes. In order to overcome this limitation in an event tagging study across different particle colliders, we have developed a novel technique that involves propagating relevance down through the layers of a neural network. Utilizing this technique, we were able to create new variables that improve event classification while offering greater understanding into the ML process. These new variables were successfully integrated into two distinct ML methods - the universal oscillator and XOS models. Utilizing the propagator, we were able to determine which features hold the most value for the oscillator model and revealed that the oscillator's effectiveness stems primarily from its utilization of key variables. Nonetheless, the XOS model benefits from a more diverse feature set, highlighting its reliance on additional information. Although the event tagging study primarily centered on understanding ML decisions, this technique has far-reaching implications that could enable the incorporation of additional theoretical variables to enhance ML performance in high-energy physics.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We introduce a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their lowest forms. We then establish formulas for these degenerate r-connected Stirling numbers and show their connection to a specific kind of polynomial, known as the degenerate r-simplicity polynomial.

The paper examines the properties of one-dimensional representations for Ash and ordinary layer groups, along with double groups associated with finite rotation symmetries. It demonstrates that constructing such representations involves an irreducible approach and highlights the importance of local symmetry in this context, specifically the cases of $C_{2v}$, $D_{2h}$, $C_{4v}$, and $T_{d}$ groups.

For a D-dimensional spacetime with Killing vector fields making up the basis for the tangent space, we can generate momentum operators by integrating along their orbits. Those that correspond to geodesic trajectories have vanishinging components, simplifying the calculation and giving rise to a new class of momentum operators. In the process, we've shown that a particular vector field corresponding to 3D spacetime, matching a known result. We've also demonstrated that the alternative method of calculating momentum operators by taking the Hamiltonian's gradient, is equivalent to using the Killing vector fields. In the case of a D = 3 spacetime with 3 independent Killing fields, we've managed to express the total momentum operator as the sum of three separate operator products.

Developing an accurate machine learning model for sign-fluctuating many-electron systems, such as those described by the Hubbard model, poses significant challenges despite the simple physics underlying these systems at its core. Previous models using real-valued units have struggled to resolve the sign problem, a issue that can be partially attributed to the restrictive nature of real-valued units. We have found that employing complex-valued units, specifically cPNPs, has yielded positive results in the past; however, the associated architecture remains unsophisticated and lacks clarity. We have refined this architecture by introducing several novel features. Firstly, we have replaced the existing circuit sampling method with a more organized and intuitive sampling approach. Secondly, we have incorporated an innovative regularization technique. Both of these enhancements have significantly improved the effectiveness of the model. Our research has shown that the improved cPNPs have achieved remarkable accuracy in the study of the ground state at half-filling in the two-dimensional Hubbard model, a notable achievement considering previous models using real-valued units have failed to accomplish this feat.

We recommend investigating the composite flavon-higgs framework as a potential
solution to address the sources of CP violation detected in neutrino oscillations
and baryogenesis. This framework is comprised of two complex scalar fields, a flavon
and a Higgs, which are both formed by a condensation of vector fermions in a gauge
mediated theory. The framework naturally incorporates a CP-odd axion, resulting from
a flavon parity breaking term, and exhibits a hierarchy of scales between the
flavon and Higgs masses, contrary to the standard model. The mechanism of mass
generation for the flavon is dubbed the "hidden sector minimal fermi-point
scattering" (HMFS) and involves a complex interaction within the scalar sector. A
simple numerical calculation indicates that the neutral flavon can be biased to a
heavy mass range compatible with the associated muon anomalies, while the charged
flavon is predicted to have a mass in the 100 GeV range, a scale that could be
adjusted for alignment with the W boson mass. A potential bonus of this framework
is the prediction of a spin-1 dark matter particle that can be observed in gamma-ray
telescopes or direct detection experiments, depending on its actual mass. A
theoretical model featuring two complex scalar doublets and an SU(2)L gauge symmetry
is proposed, which may realize the composite flavon-higgs framework. A
bonus application is that

The concept of immersivity in Virtual Reality (VR) refers to its ability to create an immersive 3D visual experience that feels substantial and three-dimensional. A feeling of presence in VR is achieved by reducing the user's perception of the technology's limitations, known as 'distal' artifacts. These artifacts arise from the user's awareness of the technology's distant nature, caused by differences between the virtual and real-world visuals, such as resolution, field of view, and projection types. This research introduces a new perspective on minimizing perceptual distortions in VR by focusing on the user's shadow. It demonstrates that the distance between the user's shadow and real-world objects can serve as a distal indicator, revealing the system's artificial nature. Consequently, the development of more realistic shadow simulations becomes crucial for enhancing user engagement and presence in VR applications. An evaluation study of shadow quality was conducted, revealing that high definition shadow rendering (with a resolution of 1080p) exceeds the capabilities of the human visual system and that factor explaining the variation in perceived quality among participants was the distance between the shadow and real-world objects. Additionally, the study found that participants' preferences for high definition over lower resolution shadow rendering remained consistent, even when the distance between the shadow and real-world objects was increased to 50 meters.

Deep learning models like BigScience multilingual language models show remarkable 
performance across 130 established languages, yet there's a large group of 115 
less commonly used languages left untouched. Our study focuses on four uncommon 
languages - Estonian, Finnish, Icelandic, and Latvian - by adapting BigScience 
models to these four languages. We investigated several approaches to bring these 
languages up to speed, evaluating different language processing techniques and 
training strategies using both zero-shot and few-shot learning methods. The results 
show that Big Science models learn to process new languages efficiently, and the 
few-shot strategy proves particularly effective in getting up to speed with new 
languages quickly.

We conducted 2D simulations of hydrodynamic mass transfer from a rapidly rotating core to a binary system, experimenting with an isothermal core that collapses and fragments, or one that migrates and collapses under the influence of interactions. In the initial simulations, the core's mass was allowed to increase as it spoke matter during the course of the computations. Our findings reveal that in situations involving mass gain, the mass distribution of smaller particles is more evenly distributed than in non-gain scenarios, resulting in a more uniform mass range per particle. Furthermore, gain systems tend to have fewer particles than non-gain systems, yet the overall mass transferred to the binary system remains comparable in both cases. Notably, speaking masses exhibit less preferential alignment in systems experiencing mass gain, suggesting less structured and less intense orbital interactions.

This research introduces the M-ar-K-Fast AutoRegressive Independent Components Analysis (M-ar-K-Fast-ARICA) algorithm, offering a faster alternative to previous ARICA implementations while maintaining computational efficiency similar to FastICA. M-ar-K-Fast-ARICA builds upon the concept of time-series compounding in Mixture-ar-K-Means Fast Clustering (Mixture-ar-K-MFC), adapting its idea to the analysis of time-series data through the creation of a Mixed AR Model. By establishing a unified framework for data representation via the quantity of non-zero elements in binary matrices, M-ar-Fast-ARICA enhances the accuracy of the FastICA method in modeling independent component relationships, effectively reducing memory usage and corresponding errors. Experimental findings using synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that M-ar-K-Fast-ARICA matches the performance of its parent algorithms but at a significantly lower computational cost.

This paper revisits and expands previous research by Khan and Blass, addressing two primary queries and offering corresponding upper and lower bounds for certain computational complexities. Notably, the research leverages finite model theory concepts, particularly the properties of set pairs in models, to analyze demonstration complexity in handling diagram distinctions. By applying a concept analogous to Baker's theorem for multivariate polynomials over algebraically closed fields, the authors demonstrate the interconnection between choices and complexity in infinite models, ultimately establishing a relationship between Choiceless Polynomial Duration and Extended Polynomial Calculus for quantifier-free diagrams.

The collection of $\sigma$-elementary rings includes nitely generated algebras over fields of characteristic zero, complemented by a demonstration that the ring of germs of holomorphic mappings is $\sigma$-elementary.

The problem of verifying the origin of data is encompassed by the concept of framework. A framework enables the identification of a data set's creation details, such as the source and time, and allows these details to be included in the data for future reference. We investigated various methods to determine the framework for a given data set, specifically a collection of human language texts, by utilizing clues present in the texts themselves. A framework is comprised of a set of guidelines, a set of rules, and a creator. We identified multiple approaches to determine the framework's guidelines, rules, and creator. Each of these aspects requires distinct attributes to be identified, so we examined different attribute sets and proposed potential solutions to determine them. A portion of our research focused on exploring possible approaches to determine the framework, consisting of evaluating various models and selecting the most suitable one. Ultimately, a strategy for determining the framework was established, alongside an explanation of why this approach was preferred over others.

The proliferation of social media has enabled the vast scale of generated data to surpass the capacity of existing data management tools, making it challenging to analyze this data for meaningful insights, especially in real-time applications. This research focuses on examining and predicting social media events, which typically involve analyzing user-generated content related to specific locations. To tackle the data management issues and enable real-time event analysis, we have developed Real-Time@STE, a system designed to identify and categorize social media events based on their spatial and temporal contexts. Real-Time@STE leverages an in-memory database to facilitate the processing and aggregation of social media data in real-time. By employing graph computation on spatial-temporal datasets, we can generate heat maps, which serve as a basis for event detection and extraction through a combination of clustering algorithms and user-defined rules. Furthermore, our event extraction method allows for parallel processing via the Spark framework, enabling scalable applications on large social media datasets.

The CMB and galaxy distributions exhibit a longstanding connection that has been consistently observed. While the CMB anisotropy power spectrum provides limited information about cosmological parameters, the three-point correlation function offers a more informative insight into these parameters. Nevertheless, the nonlinear distortions introduced by phenomena such as modified gravity or CDM fluctuations significantly affect the CMB bispectrum, rendering it difficult to interpret. We have developed a quick and efficient method for analyzing the distorted CMB bispectrum by approximating it through radial integrals of the CMB power spectrum, thereby facilitating the comparison of various models with observations under the assumption of no distorting effect. This method comes with an approximation error that can be associated with an $O(k^2)$ term in the CMB bispectrum. We have found that the approximate bispectrum values obtained using our method closely agree with the exact values obtained using standard methods, especially for higher-order bispectra where the agreement is much better. This method can be employed in future studies to investigate whether the distorted CMB agrees with observations by drawing conclusions based on the relative changes in the CMB bispectrum, rather than the absolute values, which helps to mitigate the impact of modeling uncertainties and potential systematics. Moreover, our method can be applied in studies that analyze the distorted CMB lensing bispectrum by replacing the CMB power spectrum with the CMB lensing potential.

To safeguard sensitive information and protect privacy in the face of potential threats, our research focuses on developing robust estimation methods that can function effectively even in the presence of malicious attacks. We employ an adversarial model where an adversary has the capability to manipulate data, but the target estimation algorithm remains unaware of this until an independent testing phase where its resilience is assessed. Given these circumstances, only the resilience of the final estimated results can be certified, not the intermediate calculations. We investigate two specific scenarios: estimating a parameter in a normal distribution and linear regression, and demonstrate how Bayesian estimation can be adaptive to various types of attacks while requiring minimal a priori knowledge about the adversary.

The COVID-19 pandemic sparked a significant spike in digital rumors transmitted via social media in China. These rumors were often shared through personalized messages, resembling a viral infection spreading process. Researchers studied COVID-19 related digital rumors in China from late February to early March 2020, uncovering the existence of an informal information network. The analysis revealed that digital rumors were disseminated primarily by a small percentage of highly active individuals. The investigation used data from Weibo, a popular Chinese microblogging platform, which showed that rumors spread to nearly 70% of users in less than half a day and reached their peak diffusion rate within three hours. The study found that digital rumors had a significant impact on users' beliefs, with 44% of users who had encountered the rumor earlier stating that they believed it to be true. The analysis also found that digital rumors disrupted the government's official communication efforts, reaching an equal or greater number of people despite being contradicted by verified information. The implications of the findings suggest that an informal information network can cause rapid digital rumor dissemination and have a substantial impact on public belief.

This paper investigates the effects of reducing hyperspectral dimensions on pixel categorization. While dimensionality reduction is a well-documented process, the resulting reduced hyperspectral images are often not optimized for pixel categorization tasks. In an effort to improve computational efficiency and overcome challenges posed by high dimensionalities, researchers have proposed various hyperspectral dimensionality reduction methods. Nonetheless, the implications of these reductions on pixel categorization tasks remain poorly understood. This study seeks to shed light on this gap by examining four commonly employed hyperspectral dimensionality reduction methods - Principal Component Analysis, Independent Component Analysis, Wavelet Transformation, and Random Forest - with a focus on analyzing their effects on pixel categorization capabilities. A set of carefully curated images, comprising agricultural and urban settings, were used to demonstrate the benefits and limitations of each method. The study evaluates reduced hyperspectral dimensions via three distinct metrics - classification efficiency, inter-classity variance, and representation homogeneity - with the results showing that no single method excels across all metrics.

We're proposing a unified approach to reducing various language frameworks.
Our method enables seamless translations between different models, enables
comprehension to be supplemented with generation capabilities, and paves the
way for thorough evaluations of model architectures. To demonstrate the efficacy
of our framework, we've developed a reduction path for the FEVE model, which
enables it to leverage advancements in transformer-based models, and we're
making our reduction target along with the transformed model available under an open-source license.

A newly created force field, called FF2N, has been designed to accurately simulate the initial stages of amide proton displacement in proteins and refined enzymes, by utilizing first-principles calculations. The force field successfully replicates the average amide proton shift observed in quantum studies and the rates of amide proton protonation and deprotonation seen in enzymes, thus demonstrating its effectiveness. The force field has been further validated by modeling the amide proton dynamics in native proteins and comparing its predictions to low-field NMR measurements. Finally, the force field has been applied to model the origin of the 5 ppm difference in amide proton chemical shifts between the helical and parallel sheet structures of apomyoglobin.

Deep neural networks' performance can be optimized using optimized loss functions, which can also modify their training dynamics and possibly improve classification results. This study investigates how altering loss functions impacts the training and accuracy of deep neural networks in binary classification. It addresses the question of whether there are numerous loss functions that can enhance model accuracy beyond the standard mean squared error. The research focuses on binary classification problems and explores the influence of loss functions with compensatory effects and equal variances. The findings indicate that altering the loss function can lead to accurate results that outperform the standard approach. Moreover, a potential approach to identifying loss functions is described, which suggests that binary classification problems could be solved using simple linear models trained with the logistic loss. This is supported by analyzing the relationship between the training data and labels, which can accurately predict the test set results in the examined datasets.

The four-box problem of residual interactions in parquet theory is reexamined from a more theoretical standpoint. A comprehensive diagrammatic framework is established, allowing for the reconstruction of a Hamiltonian from a molecular picture and leading to an interpretation of parquet's formalism as a Taylor series expansion of a Hamiltonian. Within this framework, a specific Hamiltonian expression is derived through a method similar to Fermi's golden rule, where the residual interaction is treated as a perturbation. It's observed that the four-box problem undergoes a sudden phase transition at a particular interaction strength. A comprehensive set of renormalization group flow equations is developed for the parquet formalism at a specified level of expansion.

We've refined ab initio techniques for simulating the emergence of exciton condensation through the combined effects of electron and phonon interactions. Our improved methods now enable the rapid self-consistent determination of all relevant variables on a finite momentum grid. Our new scheme consists of two key steps: initially, electron and phonon effects are calculated independently on discrete momentum grids, followed by the exact resolution of two coupled equations describing the dynamics of all variables and phonon potentials, with the option to adjust momentum and energy responses. Our advanced approach allows for more accurate and efficient calculations than existing challenges, particularly for multi-band materials, at the cost of slightly increased computational demands. To validate our improved method, we have successfully simulated exciton condensation in $TiSe_2$ under pressure, predicting a $k$-space area of $\sim 10^{-2} \AA^{-2}$ that matches experimental estimates, with our results for the superconducting gap and density of states at the Fermi level comparable to existing data. Our simulations indicate that exciton condensation originates from the driving influence of electron-phonon coupling on one-dimensional $p_{x/y}$ bands, with our predictions for the critical pressure and associated structural changes also in good agreement with experiments. Our study provides the first comprehensive theoretical description of a conventional superconducting process in a single-layer transition metal dichalcogenide.

Emergency responses initiated by dispatchers play a crucial role in saving lives, with dispatchers serving as central figures in emergency situations. To enhance decision-making, researchers suggest analyzing interactions between dispatchers and callers through data analysis tools. Existing solutions typically rely on pre-defined coding schemes to extract data, but these methods are often labor-intensive and restrict the scope of discoverable insights. To address these limitations, we developed a new system that employs an advanced data analysis method, incorporating natural language processing and machine learning techniques to uncover hidden patterns in emergency engagement data. By leveraging this system, dispatchers can gain deeper understanding into emergency situations, enabling data-driven decision-making to improve emergency response services.

The impact of Cooper pairs' spin on novel symmetries in superconductors is highly influential, yet its effects within non-centrosymmetric superconductors are relatively under researched.  We investigated the magnetic susceptibility in the d-wave non-centrosymmetric superconductor and found that an applied magnetic field can disrupt the center symmetry, leading to unique empty states at the Fermi level which are highly influenced by the Cooper pairs' spin. As a result, we observed a significant enhancement of the Cooper pairs' susceptibility in response to an applied magnetic field. Additionally, we found that this enhancement is consistent across different types of Cooper pair spin orientations.

In our current education system, students who have high initial abilities tend to excel, whereas those with lower abilities find it harder to catch up. A new strategy called "Minimax Education" is proposed to mitigate this disparity by setting flexible passing standards dynamiclly adjusted based on the previous academic record of each student. When students struggle in a subject, the passing criteria increases, making it easier for more students to pass, thereby reducing failure rates. Conversely, when students perform well, the passing criteria decrease, making it more challenging for students to pass, as only those who demonstrate a higher level of understanding achieve this goal. This Minimax approach is inspired by the concept of minimax regret decision-making and operates on a local scale for each subject, without aiming to optimize overall regresion scores.

The purpose of this research is to examine how the information density within music has changed over time. The study utilizes a large music dataset from the Music Information Retrieval Dataset Collection, which includes song titles from the 18th to the 21st century. Each song is analyzed using chroma spectral features and a form of statistical complexity is calculated for each time segment, allowing the data to be grouped by composer era. A comprehensive view of music evolution is achieved by overlaying the complexity levels of different time periods. The results indicate a significant increase in music complexity from the Classical period to the present day, with notable variations among artists of the Romantic and 20th-21st centuries.

We're analyzing a two-part process where a participant selects items from a group, and for each chosen item, we generate random feedback as part of a simulation. Our objective is to identify how this feedback impact on a participant's future selections as the number of choices grows. Through both theoretical calculations and computer-based simulations, we discover a pattern in how choices evolve over time and find that a specific model accurately represents the data by perfectly recreating the results obtained from simulations. By examining the underlying mathematical equations, we understand that the effects of the feedback slowly disappear over time, and ultimately, the sequence of the participant's chosen items converges towards a random arrangement that does not reflect any feedback.

This paper investigates the concept of playfulness in computational products from an engineering and lighting perspective. Lighting design encompasses not only aesthetics but also functional purposes such as orientation, safety, and ambiance. Similarly, the designers of play-oriented interactive systems can draw upon established design principles from various fields. This research explores how the design of playful interfaces is influenced by lighting and how different lighting styles affect users' interactions. By examining case studies of play-oriented systems illuminated with harmonious lighting, this study reveals how the choice of light sources, color temperature, and shades can create distinctive atmospheres and enhance users' experiences. Ultimately, this research offers a framework for designing the illumination of computational playfulness, providing guidance for future research and practical applications in this field.

A prominent challenge in machine learning is reward learning where a trainer demonstrates the desired outcome to a learner using simple examples. The trainer's instructions are conveyed as a set of preferences or a ranking of the target data. Existing studies assume the learner can instantly understand the trainer's intentions from each training example. In this research, we address a more realistic scenario where the learner receives a batch of instructions at a time and must efficiently utilize the learning opportunity. We propose a novel approach called Visually Supported Cluster Ranking to swiftly update the learner's knowledge. Firstly, we group the target data into clusters based on visual characteristics to capitalize on visually-related training examples. Secondly, we rank the centers of these clusters according to the trainer's preferences. Lastly, the learner learns to distinguish the chosen cluster from the others. Our experiments reveal that our approach accelerates learning and stabilizes its results compared to a learning method that relies on random data grouping. The duration of learning also helps to circumvent local minima. Our study employs real-world images from datasets such as CIFAR-10 and the ImageNet dataset, and evaluates the efficacy of our approach in various scenarios.

The Smyth powerpace construction has been a valuable tool for studying preorders and their continuous functions. While the method has proven beneficial, it has a significant drawback: the resulting spaces are often vast, containing the original input space as a proper subset. Researchers have suggested the concept of core-conciseness to measure the practicality of Smyth powerspaces. In this study, we expand upon this idea and explore potential criteria for the Smyth powerspace of a directed complete partial order to be core-concise. By establishing both necessary and sufficient conditions for core-conciseness, we are able to classify the Smyth powerspace of a discrete DCPo as core-concise. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between core-conciseness and the large-cardinal properties of ultrapowers and extend this concept to functions with compact graphs, introducing the notion of $\mathcal{C}$-finiteness.

We've observed aimed vortex loops in perfectly two-dimensional liquids composed of superfluid $^4$He droplets. A vortex loop's head is manipulated using an aspirator to collect more He, making it move towards a designated point on the edge of the droplet, where it gets pinched off and forms a new closed loop. The area formerly occupied by the pinched-off loop fills with He from the rest of the droplet due to an influx caused by the flow's momentum and velocity distributions changing. As the vortex density in the aimable loop decreases, so does its size. The aimable loop's size also depends on the distance from the asymptotically stable equilibrium position set by the loop's total momentum and velocity. The predicted effects from a theoretical model of aimed loops align with our experimental results.

For climate variables such as precipitation, future projections are often expressed as probability distributions rather than definitive forecasts.  By employing probability distribution forecasts and incorporating uncertainty into modeling, researchers utilize standard methodologies such as probabilistic forecasting and predictive distribution estimation to assess potential future changes.  One common framework for climate modeling involves modeling the rate of occurrence and threat intensity using parametric and non-parametric methods.  To account for spatial correlations in climate variables, researchers employ geographical modeling techniques including empirical Bayesian oracle regression and standard enhanced inverse likelihood weighting.  We build upon existing approaches by integrating machine learning forecasts into climate modeling, specifically through standardized enhanced ILW using neural network predictions.  This method improves upon previous techniques by maintaining a consistent probability distribution, removing the requirement for future data and allowing for flexible neural network designs.  We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to future precipitation projections in southwest Colorado.

The accuracy $\tau$ lepton mass measurement has become a benchmark for the consistency of the Standard Model and the accuracy of theoretical predictions within it. We assess the potential of the $\tau$-physics experiments at the electron-positron collider, ILC, for advancing our understanding of the $\tau$ mass. The precision of the $\tau$ lepton mass, which could reach 10 meV, will have far-reaching implications for the research areas of beyond Standard Model theory and lattice quantum chromodynamics. We compare the current theoretical estimates with the experimental results to illustrate the growing discrepancy between the predicted and measured $\tau$ lepton mass.

A dry baroclinic wave system in a spinning annulus is studied through both experimental and computational methods. Both approaches show strong agreement in the results. The experimental method employs a laser to induce heat in a rotating, viscous liquid contained within an annular container, which then forms dry waves due to baroclinic instability. Simultaneously, a corresponding numerical model is run using a multi-phase integration technique to analyze the system's behavior. The resulting wave patterns, as well as their associated characteristics, from both experiments and simulations are compared in several configurations involving variations in wave intensity and mean flow circulation. The testing setup is a modified version of the classic Majumdar-Gogusan design to facilitate multi-phase simulation implementation.

A widely employed method in extreme value statistics involves transforming data under reverse cumulative distribution functions to simplify the estimation of extreme risk parameters. While this approach facilitates easy calculations, it has been found to introduce significant biases, particularly notable for smaller data sets. Researchers have proposed an alternative method utilizing a Poisson process reparametrization, which combines the benefits of intuitive interpretation with precise calculations. The new estimation technique has been found to outperform the traditional transformation approach in terms of accuracy and is comparable to the best statistical models available. The proposed method has been shown to effectively estimate parameters in scenarios involving small to moderate data sizes.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on the robustness of RL algorithms when dealing with imperfect data. Specifically, we consider a specific data flaw - the presence of corrupted episodes. An episode can be corrupted by altering the reward functions of the states it contains. A single corrupted episode can lead to misclassification in the offline setting, potentially causing the RL algorithm to deviate from its optimal performance. We've developed two approaches for RL to be resilient against corrupted episodes: overconfident trajectory filtering and correlation-based filtering. These methods can be integrated into existing RL frameworks offline. We theoretically prove that these algorithms achieve near-optimal performance even in the presence of corrupted episodes. Moreover, we experimentally verified our results and demonstrated the effectiveness of our approaches on a variety of grid-world experiments.

This research examines the 1-D heat equation with dynamic boundary conditions under time-varying circumstances. By applying the concept of logarithmic curvature, we determine the theoretical manageability of the equation's initial boundary value problem, considering variable boundary conditions. This investigation also employs impulsive control to modify the equation and, through Taylor series expansion, analyzes the asymptotic nonimpulsive behavior of solutions under certain conditions. Finally, numerical examples confirm the results and illustrate how changes in impulsive intervals and frequencies affect solution behavior.

Understanding the boundaries of learning models is essential to guarantee their reliability. Out-of-distribution detection, which identifies unseen data as unconventional, is seen as a way to measure a model's generalizability. However, the lack of systematic methods for categorizing real-world data leads us to delay defining the set of out-of-distribution categories until detection methods are established. In this research, an automated process is used to group text categories and their representations are clustered based on their common characteristics. Experimental studies show that the proposed categorization has a natural association with the effectiveness of out-of-distribution detection, which confirms our method's validity. Moreover, our findings suggest that current models fail to recognize text categories as visual concepts, meaning there are many instances where these categories could be distinguished more effectively through visual inspection rather than textual analysis.

This research develops a theoretical model describing non-equilibrium Brownian molecular engines powered by inelastic electron tunneling. It places these systems within a broader framework of nanoscale machines. By applying this model, calculations were conducted for two specific scenarios: one involving a dual-well system where the tunneling current varies seasonally in response to a DC voltage, leading to continuous engine operation; a second scenario involving a three-state system displaying bistable behavior, where an external AC voltage can induce oscillating engine motion. Furthermore, the study presents findings on how an external force can impact Brownian molecular engines and influence their efficiency. It's observed that while similar concepts as in thermal molecular engines based on polyoxometalates apply, distinct characteristics exist where an optimal balance of tunneling and transport rates lead to optimal engine efficiency. Moreover, the research offers practical recommendations for experimentally validating the dynamical models proposed.

We define a concept of unidirectional resynchronizability for term transducers and establish its equivalence to several other definitions found in the literature. By building on this definition, we create a well-motivated extension of the definition to couple transducers and discuss its implications. Furthermore, we provide a method for determining unidirectional resynchronizability of term transducers from automaton representations, which leads to an algorithm for determining if a term transducer is unidirectionalally equivalent to a sequence of simple sub-transducers.

In this research, we explore the speed benefits of applying the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to compute generalized convolutions, and we show that this can be done more efficiently than a straightforward brute force approach. By leveraging the properties of FFT, we can successfully achieve a time complexity of O(NlogN), where N is the total number of elements being processed. Interestingly, achieving this O(NlogN) complexity wasn't always straightforward - it required a novel generalization of FFT. Additionally, we successfully applied our FFT-based convolution calculation to tackle two long-standing problems in combinatorial mathematics, and we found that in both cases, the answer could be represented as a rational number with a very large denominator. Finally, we proposed a practical method to simplify such large denominators by factoring them into more manageable components.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 proved that objects could exist in an intermediate state between L and T brown dwarfs. However, the nature of GJ 229B's parent object remains a source of conflict, as it was initially identified as having a spectrum that blended human and robotic characteristics. By utilizing the APOLLO retrieval code to analyze available near-infrared spectroscopy data for the system, our research aims to determine the characteristics of GJ 229B and the compatibility of its spectrum with those obtained through space-based observations. The results show that the spectrum of GJ 229B is consistent in features across multiple studies and that the objects within the system are characterized by temperatures, masses, and magnetic field strengths of about 600 K, 42 M$_{\odot}$, and 3.5 kilogauss, respectively. Our calculations indicate that the probability of the spectrum matching the late L-dwarf spectrum of GJ 229B at high confidence levels is virtually zero, and that the accumulated sedimentation of dust and clouds in the system could explain the discrepancies seen in earlier vs. later observations. The results from our radiative transfer model demonstrate that it is possible for the spectrum of the L/T transition object 2MASS 1507-16$^{\rm b}$ at temperature 595 K to display features of both L and T dwarfs, and that the system's properties are consistent with those of other objects at

The possibility of observing the $f_0^{(2)}(1300)$, a state with unique $0^{--}$ quantum properties, through the process of $\gamma \gamma$ decay, is investigated. Notably, the current data from the BaBar and Belle experiments show that their findings for this state are contradictory. While the BaBar data suggests a $f_0(1300)$ with 0.18 picobarns branching ratio for $\gamma \gamma$ decay and a mass around 2.2 GeV, against which a resonance with 0.33 picobarns branching ratio and a mass around 2.0 GeV for the same process is inferred from Belle's data. Given these discrepancies, the existence of $f_0^{(2)}(1300)$ as a physical entity is questionable. The present work examines non-trivial tetraquark state with color structure $\bar q \bar q \bar q q$ in a constituent quark model, incorporating the effects of internal confining forces. The calculations yield a branching ratio of about 0.25 and a mass around 2.0 GeV for the process $\gamma \gamma$ decay. The study also explores other possible interactions of the $f_0^{(2)}(1300)$, including $K K \bar K \bar K$, $\pi \pi \pi \pi$, and $f_0(1500) f_

We obtain theoretical predictions for the $CP$-violating quantity \phi_s and the decay width difference \DeltaGamma_s, which occur in the standard model's charmless decay of the B_s* meson. These predictions originate from a QCD factorization framework. Our analysis relies on two-body decays contributing to the mixing phenomenon, specifically on ratios of decay widths (\R_s and \R_p) derived from the amplitudes (a_1/sqrt(2) + ip) and (a_2/sqrt(6) + ip). The constants p and a_1 are determined by incorporating the vector and scalar components of the resonance. Notably, the value of a_2 is set to zero in our study. We calculate the theoretical range for \phi_s by varying the decay width ratio \Rs between 0.3 and 0.4, which corresponds to current experimental values. This results in \phi_s theoretical values between -0.695 and -0.671 rad. Regarding \DeltaGamma_s, the theoretical prediction is -0.093 ps^-1, encompassed within a range of -0.11 ps^-1 (error due to \Rs variation) and -0.077 ps^-1 (error due to the uncertainty in a_1). These findings indicate that the current experimental values could already constrain the decay width ratio \Rs and, in the absence of \DeltaGamma_s measurements, could lead to an irrational dependence

Understanding and predicting infectious disease transmission in crowded settings is essential. Researchers made observations on an urban bus, collecting a diverse set of passengers' respiratory data utilizing a sophisticated sensor technology, which enabled the creation of detailed mathematical models that accurately replicate the dynamics of disease transmission in that specific environment. By testing these models using data from past rides, scientists calculated the probability that an infectious person would transmit the disease to at least one other passenger under the same bus conditions. The results indicated a significant correlation between the predicted transmission probabilities and the passengers' respiratory rates, showing that higher respiratory rates result in greater transmission probabilities. The relationship between respiratory rates and disease transmission was then utilized to forecast and predict the spread of the disease in various environments.

Using the shell-model, researchers have calculated the beta-decay properties of $^{135}$Te and $^{137}$Te, including their half-lives and the relative intensities of the different electron orientations. The study utilized the PNLM $TPD$ matrix element from the Vignerius interaction to determine the decay probabilities. The results showed that the beta-delayed ionization of $^{135}$Te and $^{137}$Te can produce a wide range of exotic nuclei. The researchers found that the beta-decay characteristics of $^{135}$Te and $^{137}$Te are highly sensitive to the 0νββ and νβ matrix elements between the final and initial states. The results need to be corrected for the influence of the Pauli corrections at the decay point. The researchers used the Pauli corrections calculated at the PNLM to correct the beta-decay characteristics of $^{135}$Te and $^{137}$Te. The final results showed substantial agreement with the experimental data for $^{135}$Te, but more experimental data are needed to verify the results for $^{137}$Te.

A secure double auction mechanism, requiring no reserve prices, has been developed with additional features to safeguard against cheating and unfair bidding. This new double auction mechanism offers several benefits, including ensuring a fair and even distribution of bids, preventing the disclosure of sensitive price information, and guaranteeing the integrity of transactions. To maintain security, this mechanism relies on non-repudiable signatures, one-time signatures, and a pseudo-random number generator, all of which have been proven to function securely. Moreover, the efficiency of this auction mechanism has been demonstrated by a practical implementation using High Performance Linear C code, paired with an overview of its key components in terms of C language source code. Finally, a series of test double auctions have been conducted to validate the mechanism's behavior under various scenarios, in addition to a performing a comparative analysis with an unsecured double auction mechanism.

In a theoretical study, the ground state of mesons comprising a light quark and a heavy one (b or c) is analyzed using a specific framework. By comparing calculated masses to experimental values, the findings support the idea that these mesons have a distinct octet and a nonet quark structure. Additionally, an internal arrangement of quarks in these mesons is examined.

A composition of functions is a way to create new functions by alternating input and output values. Periodic compositions of real-valued functions with a specific property have been examined in relation to curves that are not only periodic but also have a limited rate of change. It has been found that certain curves with a specific scaling aspect are not non-expansive, which has implications for periodic compositions with a certain structure. On the other hand, some non-periodic curves with a specific scaling aspect are not non-expansive, which has implications for compositions involving certain types of periodic functions. Ultimately, it was found that periodic curves with a specific scaling aspect are not non-expansive, which has implications in the study of functional equations.

Dynamic mode decomposition is a popular technique for approximating high-dimensional systems with simple linear representations. However, many real-world processes exhibit nonlinear behaviors, requiring a deeper mathematical approach. Building upon kernel methods and optimization techniques, a novel nonlinear dynamic mode decomposition algorithm is developed using Clarke's generalized function, which yields an efficient and scalable solution. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through various numerical examples, showcasing its ability to capture both slow and rapid dynamics in complex systems. Furthermore, the study highlights the algorithm's robustness against inaccuracies in system modeling, a key advantage in complex and dynamic environments.

The development of chess as a computer game allowed for the analysis of vast amounts of data, enabling researchers to study the game's complex structures. To gain insights into chess strategy, this paper examines chess player discussions from the online forum Chess.com by exploring the similarities between different chess openings. Our analysis involves incorporating novel quantitative metrics: the centrality of an opening in a player's overall chess repertoire (quotient) and an opening's standard sub-groupings (codification). These metrics aid in understanding the intricacy of chess openings, reveal groupings within the classification system, and reflect the expertise of chess players. Additionally, our results demonstrate that leading chess players are associated with more complex repertoires and highlight variations preferred by top players in popular openings.

This research explores the potential internal mechanisms driving the rotation slowdown in neutron stars, specifically millisecond pulsars. Recent observations of pulsars within globular clusters indicate a higher frequency of these stars among main-sequence stars with low masses. A possible link between the slowdown of these stars and the internal friction within the stars themselves has been hypothesized. We aim to investigate this hypothesis by focusing on a specific process: the friction generated by the absorption of gravitational waves produced by a pulsar, situated at the center of a star, as it rotates rapidly. We conducted a computational analysis to determine the cutoff frequency of oscillations that can occur within the stars, allowing for the pulsar to absorb gravitational waves. The derived frequency, approximately $10^{-3}$ Hz, is in line with the rotational frequencies of neutron stars. Additionally, we discovered that the cutoff frequency is not significantly affected by other external processes such as frictional interaction with a nearby black hole. Therefore, it is likely that the frictional braking of a pulsar is the primary cause of its rotational slowdown as it rotates through the radius of its parent star. We also derive an equation to calculate the characteristic spin-down time of these neutron stars, specifically millisecond pulsars, based on their rotational frequencies and masses, as well as the cutoff frequency, which is determined by the star's mass. Notably, our analysis indicates that the spin-down times of these pulsars are significantly longer than observed in conventional supernova-spawned pulsars. The

A general approach to calculating powers of Lagrangian dynamics is outlined, 
which yields expressions for non-local quantities of motion, 
including a variational principle for the highest-order term. 
The methodology is applicable to conservative systems with n degrees of freedom, 
defined by a variable metric and a potential energy V(x), 
whose Hamiltonian is represented as H(p, x). 
The findings are demonstrated with a simple example.

This research introduces a novel task that combines elements of 3D modeling and drawing, specifically, creating 3D shapes from 2D sketches in 3D space. A key requirement is that the 3D model must match both the sketch's topology and its 2D projection. Achieving this integration poses significant challenges, primarily due to the inherent differences between 2D and 3D geometries and the need for consistent mappings.

HD 80606, a planet located about 130 light-years away from Earth, holds the record for the planet that causes the most notable changes in its host star's brightness during a transit event. HD 80606 b, a planet with an extremely eccentric orbit, passes directly in front of its host star during a transit that lasts only 2 hours each year, resulting in notable variations in the star's brightness. Observations by the James Webb Space Telescope will rely on accurate predictions for this planet to ensure effective scheduling. However, the challenges posed by the planet's highly eccentric orbit, which causes the transit to occur about half a day after predicting the time based on its periastron, make it difficult to determine the exact timing. A study used the Exoplanet Timeline Algorithm to gather transit data from various telescopes and developed a new set of predictions based on this information. A new ephemeris was also established using the available data, which revealed that the planet's highly eccentric orbit causes significant deviations from expected timing. A statistical analysis of the planet's highly eccentric orbit and the associated deviations showed that the deviations follow the expected distribution, which may be used in future studies. A test demonstrated that incorporating the data from the transit predictions into the Exoplanet Timeline Algorithm may be used in future studies. A verification testing showed that incorporating the transit predictions into the Exoplanet Timeline Algorithm may be useful.

We're investigating the behavior of an isentropic ideal fluid in the context of a specific equation of state. This particular equation states that the speed of sound varies proportionally to the square root of pressure. Our analysis reveals that when combined with the Taylor-MacLaurin series and an appropriate solution to the governing partial differential equation, the resulting series will not provide a feasible solution unless the initial data meets certain conditions related to the Hessian matrix. These conditions necessitate that the matrix's determinant and the square of its negative relative determinant have specified properties. Additionally, we've identified two distinct types of nonfeasible solutions arising from our series expansion, comprising a specific solution when the support of the initial data does not align with the Taylor series expansion and another type, referred to as a "ghost solution," which appears when certain coefficients in the series emerge as nonzero to a high degree, necessitating a sufficiently large number of terms in the expansion. Our further analysis reveals that the "ghost solution" can persist as a nonzero solution even after we formally take the infinite limit of the Taylor series, indicating that such series expansions may not suffice to comprehensively address the nature of fluid collapse for this particular equation of state.

Extremal black holes possess a unique characteristic: extremality parameter values remain constant under any spontaneous process driven by gravity. In contrast, non-spontaneous changes, such as external adjustments, cause extremality parameters to jump in discrete increments. The Iyer-Wald framework effectively captures these external modifications. By differentiating the extremality charges in relation to their values on the boundary of asymptotic regions, we deduce the prescribed variations. These variations form the basis of the amplitude under an external perturbation, as derived from the Iyer-Wald framework. For cases involving multiple charges, the amendments adhere to a systematic pattern where the largest charge dictates the perturbation amplitude. Furthermore, the extremality parameter of the smallest charge always experiences a negative change.

To optimize engine efficiency, advanced signal processing techniques are used 
to investigate the internal dynamics of engines. This research focuses on a fundamental 
question: what signals provide the most information about engine performance? 
We've analyzed various internal influences of engine performance and examined their 
impact on predictive results using the Fast Convolutional Neural Network. Our study 
shows that specific signals have a significant positive impact on prediction accuracy 
and suggests that feature reduction should be prioritized to improve engine efficiency monitoring.

A precise formulation of vibrant Poincaré symmetry is established by rigorously defining generators that are consistently boosted and translated within both space and time. This framework naturally incorporates the concept of rapidity, which is a non-local quantity derived from the Lorentz group's Lie algebra feature. We demonstrate that boosting a four-momentum quantity leads to a novel definition of mass, thereby dispensensing with the concept of independent mass and spin in the relativistic theory. We then establish a relation between vibrant Poincaré symmetry and gravity, which enables a new understanding of the latter in terms of a non-linear transformation of rapidity. Additionally, we propose a mechanism for generating massive particles through a process called 'breathing', which involves the contraction of higher-dimensional objects. A four-dimensional object that undergoes breathing transformations while being boosted gives rise to particles with both spin and mass.

Designing parameterized algorithms for graph layout problems has its challenges, especially when dealing with planarity. The conventional approach involves utilizing vertex or edge parameters, but these methods are difficult to apply to certain problems. Researchers have made progress in developing parameterized algorithms for upward planarity by focusing on specific graph properties, such as treewidth, and incorporating this treewidth as a parameter. This study explores whether graph connectivity can serve as an effective parameter for upward planarity-related problems, and it demonstrates this connection through derived algorithms and new FPT algorithms for problems that involve facilitating monotonic transformations, facilitating an arbitrary embedding, and resolving whether an embedding exists.

In visual navigation, most existing methods store and replay every experience
from training. However, this proves inefficient and ineffective. A more productive
approroach would prioritize the reuse of relevant experiences. Inspired by the
ability of humans to select memorable moments, we introduce MemoNav, an
experience-based navigation method that permits the selection of relevant
experiences for navigation. To achieve this, we designed two memory retrieval
strategies: (1) guiding the agent towards chosen experiences, and (2)
leveraging the agent's current navigation focus. Additionally, we developed a
new training method incorporating self-supervised video contrastive learning
to demonstrate the effectiveness of experienced reprocessing. Our experiments
demonstrate that MemoNav significantly outperforms state-of-the-art experience-
based navigation methods in terms of navigation efficiency and effectiveness, and
supports further extensions such as reduced experience size and increased
generalization across navigation tasks. The code is available at
\url{https://github.com/philipdudek/MemoNav}.

The demand for unbridled bandwidth and unthrottled concurrent device connectivity is propelling the mobile industry forward, thus sustaining the demand for faster wireless access. The evolution of mobile technology has been driven by the discovery of new spectrum bands and innovative solutions that enhance data rates while addressing emerging service requirements. This trend is expected to continue with the advent of 6G technology, which will address services like extremely high bandwidth, ultra-low latency, and powerful artificial intelligence support. This paper delves into the role of compact cells in the transition from 4G to 6G technology, discussing their development, the challenges they pose, and the solutions they offer. The potential applications, technical requirements, and proposed solutions for the THz band are discussed in detail.

A new concept of dynamic hypergraph framework is introduced, offering a versatile model for analyzing complex relationships in various real-world scenarios. It combines the expressive properties of hypergraphs and the flexibility of time-dependent graph modeling. We develop a comprehensive framework for measuring and capturing patterns within this dynamic hypergraph context. Specifically, we define the concepts of degree functions, independent sets, and colorings in dynamic hypergraphs, and subsequently introduce the associated framework for statistical analysis. This involves studying extremal problems related to counting, partitioning, and coloring, along with measuring symmetry and asymmetry within this context. Moreover, we develop a unifying unimodality theorem for certain counting functions across different types of hypergraphs.

We examine the relationship between two distinct representations of the intertwining operator I in the context of CFT decays. By setting the massless pole in the 3-point function to zero, we derive a relationship involving operator products, specifically a correlation function with an amputation factor for external vectors. This correlation function can be expressed as a product of two 2-point functions for operators A and B, which are connected by the intertwining operator I. Notably, the expression features operator products of A and B with an amputation factor for the massless pole. By combining this finding with earlier research on operator product expansions, we derive explicit expressions for the coefficients of local operators in A and B. Furthermore, we relate our results to state-to-state transitions in the operator bases of A and B, which are connected by the intertwining operator I. By applying a variable change inspired by σ-killing symmetry, we explore the connected nature of operator bases and 3-point function coefficients, specifically the relationships between A, B, and their associated spectra, showing these connections through examples such as $\mathcal{D}$-operators and $\mathcal{B}$-operators.

The stable Hoyle state in 4m is a key object in nuclear physics research, with existing studies dominated by perturbative methods that require confirmation from experimental data. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called the in-medium TPC method, which allows for calculating matrix elements without relying on an explicit medium perturbation theory. By applying the in-medium TPC method, we found that the 0+ to 3+ transition strength in 16O decreases from 1668 d^2 ferris wheels to 1048 d^2 ferris wheels as the density of the nucleus approaches its saturation point. Furthermore, the method's results for the Hoyle state's branching ratio exhibit good agreement with experimental data. Additionally, the method's results for the ground state's density and the Hoyle state's energy show good agreement with existing data. We also provided the method's results for the density of the Hoyle state at different density levels and the movement of the Hoyle state against density levels.

The stress-induced failure of materials that are not their usual body temperature has been extensively studied, but the similar phenomenon that occurs at a materials' inherent length scale has yet to be well understood. In a study that involved dynamically sharp notches in a 2D plane, researchers have uncovered the fact that the speed at which cracks propagate is influenced by the materials' inherent length scale, which results in the appearance of an additional frequency in the crack's motion. The resulting motion exhibits complex behavior, charactized by two distinct modes of instability, a tipping mode and an oscillating mode. The oscillating mode of instability is a previously observed phenomenon, but the tipping mode of instability has never before been reported. The relationship between the crack's speed and the materials' inherent length scale, which determines when either mode of instability occurs, is dependent on the materials' type and the crack's initial conditions. The tipping mode of instability has been found to be a transient phenomenon that is followed by an oscillating motion that is a result of an interaction between the crack tip and surrounding waves. The theory developed in this research can be applied to a wide range of crack types and is not limited to 2D or quasistatic conditions, making it a valuable tool for the study of dynamic fracture in a variety of different systems.

We examine the capacity of a discrete-time communication system where the transmitter has access to complete state information via a feedback channel connected to a discrete memoryless channel, with the receiver making decisions based on state-aware transmit symbols. We establish that knowledge of the state sequence through the feedback channel is sufficient to achieve capacity when the channel is capacityachieving and has a stochastic structure, with either the channel or input distribution being state-dependent. We also introduce an achievable rate pair by modifying a known scheme, where we utilize the state sequence to reduce entropy on the transmit side and increase it on the receive side, with both parts being state-conditional. With the modified scheme, we demonstrate achievable rates for a variety of discrete-time channels with and without state dependence. We use this modified scheme to achieve full capacity in the case of a Markov-driven erasure channel with feedback. Furthermore, we use this modified scheme to achieve a significant portion of the capacity region in the case of a state-dependent Gaussian discrete-memoryless channel. We establish that knowledge of the state sequence through the feedback channel is sufficient to achieve a significant portion of the capacity region in the case of a state-dependent Gaussian discrete-memorylesss channel. We also introduce an achievable rate pair by making two generalizations to the known single-letter achievable rate pair $(R_{\rm Q}(R_V)\cdot R_F(R_V), H(Q|F))$. With the modified scheme, we demonstrate achievable rates for a variety of discrete-time channels with and without state dependence

Researchers have observed spin-orbit interactions in various attractive fermion systems, leading to unique superfluidity phenomena. A particular class of system, the Rashba Hubbard model with strong spin-orbit interaction, has been shown to have a single-parameter set of solutions for its phase diagram. We have found that the critical line for the spin-singlet Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer phase in the Rashba Hubbard model can be transformed into a critical surface for topological superfluid phase at weak spin-orbit interaction. Additionally, we have found that the phase diagram of the Rashba Hubbard model contains two critical lines that bound the topological superfluid region. Depending on the density of the system, either of these lines could serve as the primary boundary for the topological superfluid region in the phase diagram.

This study focuses on understanding tables within scientific papers. We have established a new dataset consisting of 1,000 tables from biomedical research, along with accompanying questions that require analysis of these tables to determine whether a statement is true, false, or uncertain. Additionally, we propose an innovative task to identify table-based evidence in support of a given claim.
