Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth of a CLICTD monolithic small collection-electrode technology demonstrator using the INKA test stand at DESY, and compare it to thick sensors on fully functional CCSDA+ devices and high-thickness CCSDRC devices. Results show that the active sensor depth of the CLICTD technology demonstrator is approximately 30, in good agreement with the 30 epitaxial layer. Moreover, the team discovered that the charge collection efficiency decreased by around 50% due to the reduced sensor thickness. Nonetheless, the study suggests that the lower power consumption of the CLICTD technology could offset the decreased charge collection capability. Additionally, the study evaluates the performance of CLICTD monolithic planar hearing-aid device, which features a hearing-aid compatible design with large collection electrodes. Although the charge collection capability is limited by the thin sensor, the results demonstrate promising features, including high spatial resolution, selectivity, and quiet-time rates. Finally, the team explored the charge collection capabilities of CLICTD monolithic small-pin technology, which is designed for space applications and characterized by narrow, rectangular pins. Although the charge collection capability is limited by the thin sensor, the results showcase excellent one-dimensional resolution, quiet-time rates

Rotational shear interferometry is an established technique used to measure the velocity of the remaining uncorrected atmospheric distortions of a signal, even after it has passed through an adaptive optics system. Recent advancements in the shear interferometry technique now enable the calculation of both the velocity and direction of individual atmospheric distortion cells, making it possible to implement a self-coherent camera (SCC) technique that utilizes these cells to reconstruct an image of a target. The SCC technique has been successful in theoretical and experimental studies, but a major limitation has been the requirement for a shared beam between the target and a reference point, in order to create the distortion cells. A new method has been developed that eliminates this requirement, enabling the use of in-situ atmospheric distortion cells to restore a target image. The test showed that this method can restore ~80% of a target's original energy across ~10-20 times the diffraction limit of a 10x10 pixel image area, using a 212x212 pixel area located at the image plane of a telescope. The new method does not demand any special capabilities of a telescope or its system, making it feasible to implement this technique on various telescopes without the need to modify the existing setup.

The study examines how including a deterministic component in the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model's intercept and slope affects the probability distribution's unfavorable tail behavior. It has been established that enhancing the CIR model's deterministic component results in a more favorable risk assessment but also introduces unrealistic characteristics to the interest rate's underlying process. Consequently, a hybrid approach is proposed that combines the strengths of the "stochastic-shock" and "deterministic-shift" methods, aiming to improve the unfavorable interest rate models' capability of generating extreme negative values. Moreover, the research calculates the quantitative impact of the deterministic component on the model's long-term average and hazard rate.

Long-standing problems in neutrino oscillations remain unresolved, particularly concerning the potential existence of active-electron sterile neutrinos and the exact values of mixing parameters with other neutrinos. To address these questions, this analysis examines DUNE's capacity to detect a long-baseline neutrino beam at a few GeV energy, which could influence sterile neutrino related research fields like low-energy solar neutrinos and antineutrinos. Studying the DUNE's long-baseline experiment under these conditions reveals notable opportunities for discovering new phenomena and enhancing our understanding of existing ones within the sterile neutrino framework.

Meta-analyses allowing correlated random-effects can effectively address uncontrolled variation among studies. Yet, such models pose difficulties in estimating the variance components due to negative bias bins in the inverse-Wishart density. Consequently, this limitation restricts computational approaches, forcing some into approximate Bayesian methods. We present a new approach, however, that enables straightforward frequentist calculations, overcoming the aforementioned issue by utilizing an enhanced density modification. The proposed method enhances the asymptotic stability of estimators and maintains optimal finite-sample performance. A comprehensive simulation study demonstrates the robustness of this approach, with accompanying software availability through the R package "biascorrection".

This study introduces an innovative numerical technique for simulating complex systems composed of various particles where multiple collisions occur simultaneously. The development of this method was motivated by the limitations of existing numerical methods which either simplify particle interactions or incorporate the physical constraints of collision duration. The newly proposed multi-time-step integration method utilizes a partitioned approach in which particles interacting in the same area use the same smaller time step, while non-interacting particles operate on a larger time step. The larger time step is chosen as a multiple of the smaller one, allowing for accurate modeling of collision durations and realistic particle movements. The method's reliability was verified through numerous tests, including simulations of a particle elastically colliding with a wall, particles interacting via a short-range attraction, and clusters forming in a gas of repelling particles.

Unruh's observation that accelerated particles can't be in a global superposition of momentum states has been supported by multiple analyses. However, this observation can't be confirmed empirically due to the lack of detectable radiation. A new interpretation of Unruh's observation provides insight into its underlying meaning. This interpretation indicates that Hawking radiation is an illusion born from the interplay of measurement-induced wave function collapse and the infinite number of degrees of freedom in vacuum states. Consequently, the notion of radiation emerging from black holes through Hawking process loses coherence, revealing a more complex reality where vacuum states possess a rich structure far exceeding human perception capabilities.

The impact of the lateral momentum distribution of partons within nuclei is assessed in the context of the color dipole approach, revealing notable discrepancies between results obtained using the usual assumption of uniform momentum distribution and those found in LHC data. By incorporating a transverse momentum distribution derived from quantitative studies of hadronic reactions, we aim to reconcile theoretical predictions with experimental findings. Our analysis demonstrates that incorporating a non-uniform momentum distribution significantly improves agreement between theory and data for the case of lead-ion collisions at the LHC. Notably, incorporating non-uniform momentum distributions leads to observable differences in the photon spectrum, particularly at high photon energies and large photon angles. While incorporating non-uniform momentum distributions has a marginal effect on the photon spectrum in the case of proton-proton collisions, it has a substantial effect in lead-lead collisions, indicating its importance in understanding momentum distributions of complex nuclei.

This study presents whole number solutions for the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ under the condition that $a\neq 0$. It has been demonstrated that there are two cases which can provide whole number solutions: the first case yields an infinite number of valid solutions when $n$ is even, whereas the second case yields a single solution when $n$ is odd. Notably, all whole number solutions obtained from these cases can be expressed as a product of two matrices.

Researchers investigated the dynamics of liquid jets that enter a channel with flowing air on its opposite side. This phenomenon has the potential to improve fuel efficiency in internal combustion engines. To analyze the flow, researchers created detailed simulations using the K-Epsilon model and examined the interplay between liquid jets and aerodynamic forces. This study focuses on the physical properties of water and air and considers gravity's impact on the flow. Regardless of the angle at which the liquid jet meets the opposing surface, the interaction results in a stable and regular periodic flow pattern. This is characterized by an oscillating system in the jet's center and a rotating structure around it. Furthermore, the simulation reveals that the periodic motion is unstable in the vicinity of certain critical points. Two primary modes of instability exist: a planar disturbance that causes a shift in the oscillating system and a spiral disturbance related to the rotating structure's instability. When the liquid jet's tip reaches a certain distance from the point of impact, the disturbance modes begin to diverge and lose correlation, leading to increasingly complex behavior in the vicinity of a particular critical point in the parameter space. This research establishes a framework for identifying and understanding unstable phenomena in the flow.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on non-volatile storage for critical data protection. Crash consistency in non-volatile storage has made significant progress but remains unsolved for complex workloads, particularly those involving algorithms with covert dependencies. These hidden interdependencies can lead to data corruption and render the crash recovery process unreliable. The vulnerability of algorithms to data corruption at crash time not only affects the data integrity but also requires the development of more intricate recovery algorithms, increasing complexity and requirements. Our solution introduces an algorithm-guided crash reliability framework, allowing users to specify potential data corruption and customize recovery probability, thereby simplifying the development of reliable algorithms and enabling us to explore new possibilities for designing such algorithms.

In the current information era, vast amounts of data are generated daily from diverse sources such as social media, industrial systems, and various online platforms. Rapidly evolving industries require swift decisions based on timely extracts, forecasts, and assessments to maintain competitiveness. To effectively manage and analyze these data sets, researchers and practitioners employ information systems that incorporate expertise from multiple fields including databases, data mining, artificial intelligence, and management science. Yet, to our knowledge, the representation of hierarchical relationships within information systems has not been thoroughly investigated despite their widespread occurrence in numerous domains including taxonomy, industrial and social networks. To address this gap, we propose an expandable hierarchical model built on object-class-object associations, allowing for the modeling of hierarchical structures and enabling efficient query processing through class-based aggregation. We showcase the practical applications of this model in predictive analytics on two real-world case studies. Firstly, we examine student data from the perspective of educational institutions, utilizing hierarchical models to forecast student performance. Secondly, we analyze e-commerce data under an expandable hierarchical framework to enhance customer service representations.

We conducted an initial evaluation of the statistical forecast model based on a novel statistical theory, specifically designed to handle the complex interactions seen in chaotic three-body systems. The microstructure of the Three-Body Problem is analyzed using the flux-based approach, which informs the statistical model and enables the estimation of likelihood distributions for outcome properties. This model performs well in reproducing distribution patterns for stable orbits, but introduces discrepancies for unstable microstructures, particularly in regards to escape velocity distributions. Notably, the model excels at forecasting overall escape rates. Our study highlights the promise of this statistical model, but also identifies areas for improvement, such as developing a clearer distinction between stable and unstable microstructures to alleviate discrepancies.

To understand the mechanisms behind the decreased formation of charmonium states in heavy-ion collisions, our research investigated the yield of J$/psi$ and $D_s$ in 5.02 TeV Pb-Pb collisions, using ALICE experimental data. The suppression of charmonium states is observed across both prompt and non-prompt sources. The prompt J$/psi$ suppression can be attributed to the collision environment, whereas non-prompt D-s suppression is linked to the temperature of the QGP. Our research found that immediate and non-immediate charmonium states experience similar levels of suppression, which indicates that the formation of these states occurs over the entire volume of the QGP.

Mathematics is being employed in various tasks including computer science, biology, medicine, and astrophysics, demonstrating its vast applications beyond traditional academic settings.  The increasing reliance on sound mathematical principles for solving real-world problems in science and engineering is evident, despite the growing complexity of many hyperparameters-driven investigations which often lack solid mathematical foundations.  While Reasoning Engineering seeks to uncover the underlying logical structures of mathematical arguments, the widespread use of uncontrolled reasoning for addressing specific queries poses significant obstacles for data-driven hypothesis testing.  In light of these developments, we introduce the Continuity Theory as a unified framework for modeling reasoning patterns that evolve over time and are influenced by new discoveries.  The theory is comprised of four fundamental components - type theories, domain specific languages, metamathematics, and categorial calculus - which are adapted from existing ideas such as Isomorphism Theory.  We then develop a category of continuity with the goal of formalizing the concept's essential properties and their implications on reasoning strategies.  Throughout the paper, we present concrete examples of reasoning patterns in both real and complex numbers.

One of the key challenges in testing a software framework lies in choosing a relevant test scenario, as this determines the scope of the testing process. Unfortunately, determining the number of scenarios required to ensure the framework's correct operation proves to be a complex mathematical problem, which upon identified as an n-phased traveling salesman problem, upon further analysis was found to contain 2 n distinct optimal solutions on average. This paper proposes a parallel algorithm for determining the optimal test scenarios, leveraging the unique vector representation technique to break down the problem into multiple interconnected parts, which are then solved simultaneously to yield the final scenario set. Experimental results confirm that the proposed algorithm exhibits linear scalability on multi-core processors. A concrete example illustrates the algorithm's application in testing a search engine framework.

Many individuals who express suicidal ideas don't receive the mental health treatment they need. Suicidal thoughts are often linked to mental health conditions, but the data collected from patients typically involves multiple source information that needs to be integrated to forecast such thoughts. In this research, we present novel deep learning architectures that combine data from the medical and psychological histories of patients to predict suicidal thoughts. We utilize time series information from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) alongside free-text records of clinicians' notes to identify high-risk patients. Our frameworks leverage the sequential connections in EHRs and clinicians' notes, outperforming traditional machine learning methods and a baseline neural network.

Our research reports a definitive outcome from the Chandra and XMM-Newton space telescopes' joint observation of Cassiopeia A, along with the results from the Chandra/XMM-Newton/IXPE joint-toothless observation of this supernova remnant. Our study focused on the very energetic rays emitted by the remnant's core, which is the leftover of the massive star that exploded. Specifically, we recorded the polarization of X-ray light emitted at 3-6 keV within a tiny 2" radius area centered on the remnant's core. Our sensitive measurement indicates a significant polarization of $6.1\pm0.9$% at 95% certainty, which supports the theory that the major explosion force responsible for the core's ejection came from the rapid spinning of the core's material. Additionally, our results from IXPE, XMM-Newton, and Chandra at 5-6 keV show a notably lower polarization of $0.7\pm1.1$%. Our findings support the concept of two types of energy release occurring at the core of supernovae, namely the rapid spinning of the core (resulting in the highly polarized rays) and the interaction of the core with nearby gas (resulting in the loosely polarized rays).

Consider a set $\Sigma$ consisting of distinct, single-digit natural numbers. Erdos posed a question regarding the minimum size of $\Sigma$ such that all possible sums of combinations of its elements differ from one another. This problem was initially solved by Katona and Schopf, who determined the optimal lower bound under certain conditions. This paper presents additional insights and modifications to their work, exploring the impact of grid constraints on sum uniqueness.

In the context of dense stellar substances, the Adamopoulos-Harko-Mello-Rodrigues equation governs sound behavior within an atmosphere surrounded by negative pressure. This paper presents a revised Adams-Harko equation in a more manageable form and explores its adiabatic sound speed variant. Furthermore, we utilize this sound speed profile to establish a viable equation of state for dense stellar matter and calculate corresponding mass-radius relationships. Our findings demonstrate that the newly derived Adams-Harko equation yields compact star models in accordance with theire observed properties in Newtonian gravity framework.

This work introduces the concept of a comprehensive quantum system known as the 'compass system', which consists of linked squares of varying sizes assembled in a grid pattern, represented by the Knuth-Weyl algebra. The system's states are defined as the elements of the squares. By exploiting the properties of the algebra, a complete set of eigenvalues can be obtained, allowing for the precise characterization of all possible compass configurations in terms of the squares' diagonal and anti-diagonal elements. The maximum and minimum possible values of these elements define a dual system, enabling explorations of compression and shifting transformations among the squares.

The interfaces between gas and liquid phases in two-phase systems serve as hyper surfaces, which require in-depth characterization to extract relevant information for various applications. This paper introduces a technique for generating skeletons from interface data, which provides a simplified representation of hyper surface structures, ultimately leading to more efficient and adaptable solutions. The proposed skeletonization method is adaptable to different interface representations and allows for the detection of features without the need for prior knowledge. Furthermore, the technique can be combined with techniques for extracting closed structures, which will be discussed in a companion paper.

Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit motor activity by rolling across the cellular surface via symmetrical membrane remodeling processes. This behavior facilitates virus propulsion through mucus and enhances infection efficiency by enabling the virus to travel along cellular protrusions. A recently developed model for viral motor function in C-respved viruses is being adapted to include the role of capsid elasticity. This revised model predicts that increased capsid rigidity actually enhances viral motor speed, contrary to expectations. However, higher levels of viral elasticity may lead to abnormal viral shapes and impaired motor function. Furthermore, introducing fluctuations in viral size could potentially cause malfunctioning viral motors to recover by increasing their operational speed. Although the proposed model focuses on C-respved viruses, its underlying mechanics are likely applicable to a broader range of enveloped viruses.

Galaxies with U-shaped warps in their disks exhibit distinct distorting influences, whether it's an internal or external force causing their shape. By analyzing the morphology of 121,000 galaxies from the Dark Energy Survey, we identified 7,100 galaxies with U-shaped warps and categorized their shapes. We observed that "Jellyfish" galaxies, characterized by their extended gaseous tails, have a higher probability of having U-shaped warps compared to other galaxies. Approximately 50% of "Jellyfish" galaxies in our sample displayed U-shaped warps. We also found that galaxies with U-shaped warps are more frequently found in clusters and groups of galaxies. The ratio of major to minor axis is used as a measure of warp distance, and we found that this measure does not vary based on the orientation of the warp. This suggests that the distortion is uniform across the galaxy's shape. Furthermore, we found a positive correlation between the distortion of galaxies and the classification of galaxies with spiral arms. Higher classification values of galaxies with spiral arms are more frequently found in groups and clusters and have a greater probability of having U-shaped warps compared to those with U-shaped warps that are isolated galaxies.

This paper proves a version of the Liouville theorem for dimension $n\geq 3$ on Ricci diminutives of manifolds with non-negative curvature. The proof relies on previous work concerning the Liouville theorem for Ricci minimizers with non-negative curvature. Utilizing this result, we derive a version of the first Chern-Gauss-Bonnet theorem for Ricci diminutives of compact manifolds with non-negative curvature, as well as a Liouville theorem for Ricci diminutives of complete gradient shrinking Ricci flow solutions in dimension $n\geq 3$.

To clarify the main features of the E$\llcorner$-point anomaly observed in the phonon spectrum of ABi$_2$ (A=K, Rb, Cs) at low temperatures, the authors propose an electronic model where the bending of phonons is associated with an (E$\llcorner$)$\times$(heavy hole band) transition. The predicted phonon hardening upon cooling for RbBi$_2$ and CsBi$_2$ agrees with observed trends, whereas for KBi$_2$, this model fails to account for phonon softening as temperature increases. An alternative electronic structure for KBi$_2$ is presented where the (E$\llcorner$)$\times$(valence band) transition causes phonon softening. The proposed vibration directions and timelines explain the observed anisotropic and temperature-dependent behavior of the superconducting critical tunneling ratios at the (E$\llcorner$,0) point.

We examine how nonadiabatic Born effective coefficients relate to the volume they occupy in the context of metals. By using this insight, we establish a practical method to calculate Born coefficients in metals. By simulating the expansion of a metal Lattice and calculating the electronic energy within it, we obtain the nonadiabatic Born effective coefficients for the electronic degree of freedom. We discovered that in many cases, the nonadiabatic Born effective coefficients are closely related to the static ones, with the main variation arising from the volume in which they operate. This finding also offers a potential explanation for a common approximation made in the static case. We also investigated the variation of the Born effective coefficients for the phonon degree of freedom and found that in the adiabatic approximation the variation of the local charge is the primary factor contributing to the Born effective coefficients. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the mass associated with the Born effective coefficients is equivalent to the sum of the Drude masses for electrons and holes. By calculating the nonadiabatic Born effective coefficients for Sn, Pb, Na, K, P, Si, and Ge, we further validated the relationship and provided the mass associated with these coefficients.

Following the model of d'Obrenovic, Bocabi and Breugem, it is argued that the the nature of turbulent flows can be understood by considering both the thermal disturbance and the behavior of the thermal spectrum. It is proposed that the thermal spectrum can be broken down into three distinct ranges characterized by different types of turbulence: a smooth and uniform area far from the source, a middle region affected by thermal disturbance, and a highly turbulent and disordered space close to the source. By analyzing these ranges, it is possible to gain a deeper understanding of the dynamics of turbulent flows, particularly the behavior of waves at the interface of the middle and disordered regions where the turbulence assumes a glass-like structure.

We've discovered a novel topological phenomenon characterized by a time-reversal invariant that is nonlinear in the magnetoelectric coefficient. The driving force behind this reaction involves the interplay of two distinct elements: the generation of a magnetic monopole and the emergence of a $\pi$-flux. Like the Witten effect, this reaction executes a parity transformation on magnetic monopole quanta. Furthermore, the magnetoelectric coefficient exhibits a half-integer value when bound to a particular topological state, synonymous with the occurrence of a topological phase transition at zero magnetic field. The proposed model is supported by observations of the non-linear magnetoelectric reaction, the half-integer value of the magnetoelectric coefficient, and the emergence of novel topological states in the Hofstadter spectrum.

In delayed feedback systems, a small-timed lag modulation applied to the feedback path can exponentially boost the unfolding pseudospectral gap. This amplification effect is equally present for both positive and negative delays, potentially leading to massive error propagation. We have discovered two mechanisms contributing to this phenomenon. Firstly, the dynamic interaction between the delay and minor perturbations creates a chaotic distribution of delay values. Secondly, the rapid spectral degeneration due to the varying delay results in an extremely high potential for unfolding. Notably, the cost of this amplification is extremely low, making it a potentially significant factor in the behavior of delay systems across various fields, including physics, engineering, biology, finance, and electronics.

This paper introduces a type system for the probabilistic lambda calculus that leverages a novel notion of types with optimal quantification. Our type system ensures that the probabilities of well-typed terms are evenly distributed. Furthermore, we define a corresponding model consisting of sets equipped with measures and establish that it is sound relative to the type system.

Design communication often employs various media like verbal, written, and visual interactions. Effective communication hinges on utilizing suitable languages for the respective media, matchinng audiences to the appropriate languages, and consistently applying those languages to avoid and clarify any misunderstandings that may arise. Historically, different design disciplines have used distinct terminologies despite some overlapping words, thus posing challenges for cross-disciplinary collaboration. A new concept, "conclusion stability," is introduced to ensure reliable conclusions can be reached regardless of the specific language used to convey design conversations' content. Empirical studies were conducted across three design subjects - architecture, art, and landscape design - by first establishing statistical models to establish correlation between disciplinary specific terms and their co-occurring concepts, and subsequently compiling vocabulary trees to facilitate the creation of stable conclusions. A test case demonstrated the practical application of this concept in generating stable conclusions from design conversation's semantic representations. The proposed framework aims to bridge the gap between different design paradigms and enable the creation of stable conclusions from diverse design communication sources.

We suggest an approach to understanding the origin of gravity at a very early stage in the universe. This theory proposes that gravity emerges from a interaction between coherent Higgs-Goldstone fields and the detectable "footprints" of retro-causal de-coherence in the quantum states of space-time itself. his hypothesis is based on the concept of space-time itself being in a super-position of ordered and disordered states until observed, and the detection of order parameter values acting as a "memory' that retro-causally influences the initial quantum state of the universe. Furthermore, the universe's gravitational dynamics can be explained by the interactions between these order parameters and the detuning of space-time's quantum phases. This model naturally predicts the existence of 'gravitons' as long-wave fluctuations in the space-time tensor fields. Given the nature of this theory, it presents a challenge to conventional differentiations between "matter" and "geometry", and instead, it can be seen as an extension of the holographic principle in the context of the vacuum state of Higgs-Goldstone fields.

We introduce a novel method for optimizing functions of several variables, one of which is constrained to be non-negative. This optimization method differs from the standard Lagrangian method in that it relies on a non-negative variable that is shared across multiple constraints, rather than using separate multiplier variables. Instead, the new method utilizes a gradient-based optimization technique that incites soft constraints to soften at sensitive points. As a result, the non-negative variable will only take on a value of zero if it is already zero, eliminating unnecessary oscillations. The surface of non-zero values is accurately mapped, enabling a range of new applications including directing sound waves at resonant frequencies and pinpointing the source of oscillations in a complex system.

We are introducing a new concept of feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within the context of associative rings. A prime ideal in an associative ring is considered feebly $1$-absorbing if any three non-zero ring elements whose product is from the ideal's multiplication, also have their sum equal to $1$. The properties and characteristics of these ideals have been investigated and it has been established that feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals exhibit all the characteristics of universally $1$-absorbing prime ideals. Moreover, a feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideal in a commutative ring is identical to a prime ideal that is also feebly $1$-absorbing.

We present new findings for two semileptonic decay processes, $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and a lepton-neutrino pair, and $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$ with the same pair, utilizing data from Belle II's sample equivalent to 189 inverse picobarns collected using the SuperKEKB $e^-e^+$ collider. To identify these decays, the research used the recoil $B$ meson's hadronic transitions into various final states, then analyzed the energy spectrum of the lepton, neutrino, and hadronic systems to determine branching ratios and aid in kinematic parameters. The study reports a measurement of $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-(\to \pi^-\gamma)$ and a lepton-neutrino pair with a branching ratio of $(4.2\pm0.6\pm0.3_{stat}\pm0.3_{syst})10^{-4}$, and a branching ratio for $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0(\to \pi^+\pi^-)$ and a lepton-neutrino pair of $(3.8\pm0.6\pm0.3_{stat}\pm0.3_{syst})10^{-4}$. These results align with theoretical predictions.

Our team developed a solution to rapidly cross-match sources using a planar optical device that can process multiple channels simultaneously, and we've combined this with an algorithm that utilizes spectral similarity. This enables the rapid identification and characterization of objects with similar spectral features across vast astronomical datasets. Built with integrated optics and refined through mathematical modeling, our device features distinct fingerprinted features that enable high distinction between sources and reduce errors. We've implemented and tested this solution using a library of optical filters and a database of spectral curves. This technology offers an innovative approach to applying advanced algorithms in spectroscopy through the integration of multi-channel optical processing and spectral analysis.

The increasing availability of medication data, as shown in databases such as the FDA's Anatomical Therapeutic Classification (ATC) code, holds great potential for enhancing healthcare through data-driven analysis of medication interactions. Nonetheless, current methods for interacting medications are generally restricted to pairwise analyses, overlooking the intricate interconnections among larger groups of medications, such as those classified under the same ATC codes. In this study, we introduce a novel framework that employs a cohesive perspective to model these interactions among multiple medications within the same code. As a result, medications within the same code are drawn closer together in the latent representation space, accurately capturing their inherent chemistry interactions. Our experimental findings, conducted on real-world datasets covering both benefits and side effects, consistently demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed framework over existing pairwise models.

When training models to identify road damage in the GgM dataset from Germany, 
considerable performance degradation occurs when applying those models to the 
CHGDataset from China or the DUTRoadNet dataset from China. This deterioration 
arises due to the diverse damage types and complex road environments present 
in real-world datasets, which often fail to account for the comprehensive range 
of damage present in the GgM dataset. To address this issue, we employ transfer 
learning strategies, including feature extractor freezing and partial network 
retraining. Our experiments yield a mIoU score of 40.64% on the GgMDataset when 
using a partially retrained ResNet-50 model, surpassing the original score of 
38.04%. We also establish a timely benchmark for real-world road harm identification 
in the United States by evaluating our model on the recently released MRRGDataset. 
In comparison to existing models, our approach achieves an mIoU score of 35.43% on 
the MRRGDataset, showcasing its superior performance relative to state-of-the-art 
models. Ultimately, we release our source code and pre-trained models to facilitate 
advancements in this field.

We've developed a novel deep generative approach called mimicry that enables
the creation of distinct forms of discourse from observed examples in one
domain and producing new discourse in another domain. For instance, we can
generate news titles based on comments from Reddit's r/dailycommenters and
create new political debates based on discussions from Politifact. Our model
learns to produce human-like text by examining sequences of text as a
combinatorial markov process, using the advanced structure of language
reinforced through adversarial training, and applying a form of data-driven
language acquisition to discover new forms of discourse. The model produces
newswer text samples, as demonstrated in our political and news title
generations, and significantly outperforms existing deep learning methods
for multiple domains.

A massive Population III protostar develops an intense magnetic field, which plays a significant role in the surrounding accretion disk's fragmentation and the star's mass-ejection properties. We investigated how this magnetic field affects the flow of gas into the protostar using a set of realistic models, which take into account the dynamic movement of magnetic fields and the no-scattering assumption. As the protostar grows in mass, its magnetic field expands and becomes more turbulent, which causes it to lose energy and eventually dissipate into the surrounding disk. This process leads to an exponential increase in magnetic field strength with radial distance from the protostar. Our studies reveal that within a few hundred stellar radii from the protostar, the magnetic field is strong enough to halt gas flow into the accretion disk, effectively preventing the disk's fragmentation and the protostar's mass loss through jets. However, larger-radius disks remain unstable and undergo the fragmentation that gives rise to additional protostars and masses lost through jets. Ultimately, our model indicates that the total amount of mass lost through jets is the result of a delicate balance between the effects of magnetic field dynamics and disk properties, which in this case leads to an upper limit of 0.1 solar masses lost through jets.

Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves comparing credit card behavior to identify unusual purchasing patterns. Although the discovery process for association rules is well established, the task of reducing the resulting number of rules receives relatively limited attention. In this research, we explore how to reduce the complexity of the resulting rule sets by leveraging inference schemes. This approach allows us to identify new rules based on existing ones and is relevant to minimal-size base generation. By combining inference schemes, we can create compact representations of large rule sets. Our analysis focuses on how to select the most relevant inference schemes to produce the most efficient minimal-size bases. Since the injection time of schemes varies significantly, as does the impact of their combination, we developed an averaging method to determine the optimal performance. Our findings, driven by observations from credit card data, demonstrate the superiority of minimal-size base-based analysis over straightforward rule sets.

Imprisonment necessitates the incorporation of a criminal justice system, yet it frequently overlooks the profound emotional impact it has on those within it. Specifically, this paper investigates the effect of mandatory mental health treatment on the well-being of incarcerated individuals, taking into consideration the inherent coercive nature of such treatment. By doing so, it achieves two objectives: first, it clarifies the ethical implications of forced therapy on psychological well-being, incorporating the perspectives of human rights defenders who oppose the practice; second, it explores the utility of mental health treatment as a tool for enhancing the mental health of those within the criminal justice system, thus positing that its provision does not necessarily legitimize the system's coercive elements.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine their properties and relationships, and establish connections to other notable polynomials.

Cellular network service quality can vary significantly depending on location, which is crucial to understand for managing spectrum resources efficiently. Rapidly developing technologies like massive MIMO, MEC, MBB, and 5G are driving the need for precise knowledge of spectrum distribution. Current methods for spectrum analysis are often labor-intensive or restrictive, which hinders their practical application. In this study, we explore the potential of utilizing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) by introducing a novel aerial spectrum observation approach called AESO. Using the radio downlink signal, AESO estimates the spectrum coverage map and evaluates its quality. To facilitate this, we develop a radio downlink signal model and an adaptive UAV positioning strategy. Our results demonstrate that each UAV contributes equally to the map estimation and that two to three UAVs are sufficient to obtain a high-quality map. This finding offers valuable insights for designing efficient UAV spectra observation strategies.

This paper tackles the anomaly detection challenge, a prominent issue in the broader field of predictive maintenance. The paper demostrates that an existing anomaly detection method can be applied to data sequences, even if the start and end points of these sequences are uncertain. To achieve this, the paper proposes an alternative approach, incorporating the gauge probability of Hidden Markov Models in multiple ways. A numerical example compares the proposed method with the existing anomaly detection method, revealing that the latter method treats data sequences as complete and aligned, which may lead to distorted results.

To effectively tackle authentication-related issues in secure access control and safeguard personal information, a multimodal authentication system was designed and improved, which uses audio-visual-thermal information and was tested with 150 subjects. The system's performance was evaluated using FAR (False Acceptance Rate) and FRR (False Reject Rate) as metrics, and the results showed its strong authentication capabilities: a 0.13% FAR and a 0.01% FRR at a 95% confidence level when the authentication distance is 5 sigma. The study found that combining the three modalities yielded better results compared to using two or one modality alone. Furthermore, the results demonstrated that our system's performance improved as the authentication distance increased.

Most current speech translation systems are trained using data augmentation techniques that require significant adjustment to existing models and high-quality reference sentences. We introduce an efficient method to train speech translation systems directly from extended transcriptions without needing to update the model architecture. This new method enhances data quality by allowing multiple translations of extended transcriptions to be generated with low computational cost. Our method brings two key benefits: it substantially decreases the effort required to prepare speech translation data and makes more relevant information available to the model. Our experimental findings confirm that this new method leads to superior performance compared to conventional data augmentation techniques and the baseline model. Specifically, it achieves a significant improvement of 2.3 and 1.3 WER reduction on the WSJ dataset and 2.0 and 1.2 BLEU increase on the IWSLT en-de dataset.

A nonparametric approach has been developed to estimate the average composition of individual components in mixtures based on separate measurements of their properties. This method, rooted in unbiased estimation, relies on maximum likelihood estimation principles and is applicable with or without knowledge of the true distribution of the mixtures' properties. The proposed estimator operates by comparing the properties of each component with simulated values from the true mixture distribution, with weights reflecting the number of observations per component. When applied to a binary blend of metals detected through X-ray fluorescence, the method demonstrated acceptable accuracy. Furthermore, the estimation method was successfully used to determine the mean parameters of particle sizes in medical plaque samples and color measurements in images, with and without prior knowledge of the true distribution.

Achieving balance between disclosing useful information and protecting sensitive data has driven the development of Differential Privacy. This study examines a specific scenario where the data set contains pairs of interdependent information. For instance, a data set might include both a person's income and spending habits. We found that conventional DP enhancements fail to provide satisfactory privacy protection in such cases. As an alternative, we introduced the Dependent DP framework, which incorporates functional dependencies into the DP metric. Furthermore, we proposed the DP Loss of Information and adapted the established privacy evaluation methods for dependent characteristics. Finally, we provided algorithms to calculate the DP Loss of Information for various common dependencies.

In the As 209 system, we discovered a distinct CO void at 13-15 au by combining the submillimeter colors of the circumstellar disk derived from the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-creating Scales (MAPS) project, and the high-resolution images from the ALMA Pilot Project. As a result, we identified two possible explanations for the CO void. Firstly, CO depletion due to snow settling into the disk midplane could account for the void's appearance, but this would require a significant reduction in CO abundance within the top 10-20 au by at least an order of magnitude. Alternatively, CO transformation into more stable species like CH3OH, which is found in the disk's snow line region, could be a plausible alternative to explain the void's existence. Our findings emphasize the need for further investigation into the carbon chemistry in the As 209 system, particularly through spectral line observations that can distinguish between various carbon-bearing molecules.

This paper introduces an advanced software toolkit designed to efficiently process and compare time-stamped data from various sources, such as simulation models, analytical tools, and real-world measurements with varying time resolutions. The research highlights the benefits and limitations of existing data analysis tools and outlines our approach to developing a versatile, platform-independent solution with a wide range of features, including: comprehensive data visualization capabilities; sophisticated data manipulation and analysis tools; support for the evaluation of statistical significance; robust data alignment and comparison functionalities across different time resolutions; and a user-friendly interface that facilitates easy and effective data evaluation. We illustrate the toolkit's versatility through two practical case studies examining the impact of two distinct agents on a specific system.

We establish the existence of smooth and varied solutions in average field games of controls with state constraints from the initial data of a Banach space, under the condition that the constraints are confined to a compact and convex neighborhood.

Stellar threads in the Milky Way's plane exhibit narrow magnitude distributions and possess resolved counterparts in the Gaia dataset, contradicting their initial descriptions as faint, extended objects in the plane. Re-examining the definition and classification of stellar threads reveals that distinguishing them from other objects in the Milky Way's plane relies solely on their low surface brightness. This leads to a proposal for a new classification system for stellar threads based on their low surface brightness, narrow magnitude distribution, and Gaia data consistency, which would apply universally to all galaxies. Within the new classification system, two types of stellar threads exist: those that are resolvable into individual stars through Gaia and those that are not. Utilizing this new framework, a study was conducted to search for the two types of stellar threads within the Milky Way's bulge and plane, utilizing Gaia Data Release 3. The results show that distinct populations of stellar threads exist in the bulge and plane. A tight concentration of readily distinguishable stellar threads exists within the bulge at approximately 10,000 light-years from the galactic center, whereas a broader distribution of these stellar threads exists in the plane. However, this separation decreases when considering the second type of stellar threads with low surface brightness, which are identifiable through Gaia. In contrast to the first type, these stellar threads show a planar distribution and are characterized by larger uncertainties in their derived parameters.

The problem of visual inconsistency detection, crucial for completing incomplete image data in various applications, has been tackled in this research. A custom dataset, eFashion, has been created to facilitate this project by recruiting users to identify inconsistencies in random outfit combinations. A specific outfit ensemble is defined as a sequence of images displaying the same items of clothing in different ways. A pre-trained transformer model, trained using eFashion, is then employed to extract visual features from the outfit ensemble, which are subsequently analyzed to predict whether an inconsistency exists in the displayed images. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed approach surpasses competing methods in visual inconsistency detection while also demonstrating the benefits of using a pre-trained transformer on fashion-specific data. When applied to the standard dataset, OI, the model shows improved performance with a higher F1-score of 0.067, as opposed to the current best score of 0.056. Furthermore, the model has successfully generated an API that is now operational on the eFashion platform, providing free inconsistency detection services to the fashion industry.

Experiments in nonclassical light have proven its numerous practical applications, however, the underlying framework for coherently evolving quantum-electromagnetic fields remains poorly understood. This study introduces a range of asset theories that can effectively model nonclassical light, using d-stable sets of probabilities and functions. By attaching value to antennas and viewing nonclassical light as assets, the theories offer insights into its characterization and measurement. The overview discusses the various asset theories, highlighting their distinct approaches and the corresponding field structures, but due to the limited existing knowledge in this field, the discussion remains preliminary and is expected to be developed further in subsequent studies.

A new aggregation method is proposed to simplify the federated averaging process and boost its efficiency. The current implementation involves buffering local gradients before sharing them with the server and waiting for the server's aggregated gradient. Our proposed approach allows gradients to be shared immediately after optimization steps from each client, eliminating the need for synchronization and buffering. This method retains the same convergence rate as traditional Federated Averaging while achieving faster training times in practical scenarios.

This research explores the joint operational calculus in the context of the algebra of polynomial tempered functions. We define the polynomial tempered distribution and its corresponding differentiation and translation operators. Building on these definitions, we develop a framework for symbolic function solutions to partial differential equations. We also examine key properties of the operators and tackle issues surrounding their composition and inverse. Furthermore, we establish a crucial identity involving the identity operator, which has implications for understanding the relationship between discrete and continuous versions of the operator.

In a previous study, the concept of the obscure dimension was explored through its interaction with a regular three-dimensional realm. Key discoveries included the existence of a critical threshold known as the Jordan perimeter, safeguarding the integrity of matter contained within the obscure dimension; evidence suggesting the obscure dimension has a vast, infinite surface area despite being subdimensional; and the emergence of fractal properties across the obscure dimension's map. Furthermore, a model based on a conventional 3D realm and a perpendicular obscure dimension can be compared to a 3D realm with infinite resolution and arbitrarily small features. Building on this work, a new understanding of primordial black holes is developed, where they compose a substance with specific properties. It has been determined that the observed dark matter fraction, approximately 4.8 times 10^-5, is equivalent to the cumulative cross-sectional area of all primordial black holes in the universe, with a radius of 10^10 cm. This model also allows for a new estimate of the total number of planets supporting complex life in the universe, where it is postulated that the obscure dimension's map will serve as a metaphorical tool for uncovering this number.

A static liquid raft is comprised of a thin layer of fluid whose surface is trapped between two rigid plates, separated by a distance that is much smaller than the characteristic length of the films bridging the gaps between floating objects. When this gap distance is smaller than the persistence length of the films, which is a measure of elastic energy over length, the raft undergoes a fracture-like transition as the gap size approaches a critical value known as the 'fracture point.' At this critical point, the ratio of mechanical energy to the energy of cross-linking between films reaches a critical value of approximately four, marking the onset of a fractal pattern consisting of highly stretched films bridging isolated clusters of objects. Our findings apply equally to static and dynamic situations, with dynamic stability dependent on the balance between external forces and the elastic energy of cross-linked films.

The conductivity of p-type III-nitride semiconductor materials is primarily limited by the low hole mobility and generation rate associated with gallium nitride. In this study, an experimental investigation focused on the anisotropic strain effects on the transport properties of gallium nitride was conducted, utilizing the lattice parameters of two alternative materials, ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$, as guides. Our data demonstrate that aligning gallium nitride with these two materials results in enhanced hole generation rates and increased mobility. Our findings can be attributed to the anisotropic strain distorting the lattice structure of gallium nitride and altering the energy levels associated with the valence band. Our research also identifies the optimal alignment angles for both materials and predicts that similar strain optimizations could improve the performance of other wurtzite semiconductor materials.

Marine robots face significant challenges in navigating through complex and dynamic environments, such as strong currents and thermal gradients that affect their buoyancy. Historically, Gaussian Processes (GPs) have effectively modelled these phenomena by considering spatial correlations, while other factors have often been disregarded. Nevertheless, GP regression suffers from a time or index shift issue, interpreting parameter values as relative rather than absolute quantities. Furthermore, GP regression models often result in smooth distributions that may not accurately represent the actual state space due to over-smoothing. To address these limitations, we introduce the Sparsified Gaussian Process Regressions (SGPR) approach, using multiple sources of information to determine the optimal correlation length scales through robust negative log likelihood optimization, thereby addressing the GP covariance matrix singularity and resulting in sparse posterior distributions that provide a more detailed understanding of the state space. By applying SGPR to low-frequency changes in sea temperature variations, we successfully conducted a sea temperature-based navigation trial, demonstrating the method's effectiveness.

This paper builds upon the findings of an earlier study (starting from page 385) to derive formulas for the Darboux and Calapso transformations of isothermal surfaces when expressed in linear potential form. Additionally, the paper demonstrates that a specific class of isothermal surfaces can be mapped to a particular subset of hyperbolic surfaces consisting of certain types of holomorphically stressed membranes.

We examine three distinct cases of nonparametric estimation for a single regression function and discuss how local averaging methods can influence its estimation. By conditioning on an optimal number of covariates and allowing the remaining variables to be used in the estimation, we can obtain consistent estimates of the regression function. Specifically, under certain conditions, these estimators demonstrate rate of convergence comparable to that of independent data estimation. Furthermore, our research explores the effects of dependent data on nonparametric estimation and extends the scope of applications for this method to include conditions beyond those initially identified in the literature. By doing so, we are able to provide more precise error estimates for our estimators. The specific results presented in this study pertain to conditionally linear regression models and smooth conditional variation scalar functions, which are estimated using kernel methods.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on the $\lambda$-versions of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. We explore and define related concepts, establishing recurrence relations and identifying abelian versions of these concepts. We also examine specific cases, expressing them in terms of $r$-Stirling numbers of the first kind.

The area of study that focuses on temporal knowledge graphs is extremely significant, as it has the potential to greatly benefit various applications in both industry and academia by providing insights into events that are linked in time. Current advancements in connection prediction for temporal knowledge graphs are hindered by the challenge of retaining time-sensitive information and consistently updating models. This research addresses that gap by introducing TP-TGN, a non-fixed model for temporal knowledge graph embedding that incorporates time-sensitive information and ensures consistent updates through the incorporation of time into the distribution of event vectors. However, since fixed models have inherent advantages when it comes to handling changes in the distribution of event vectors, this research also investigates the feasibility of utilizing fixed models for connection prediction in temporal knowledge graphs by adapting them to fit the time-based distribution of event vectors. The evaluation results conducted on the Temporal Knowledge Graph Kernel and the Wide Area Temporal Knowledge Base reveal substantial improvements when utilizing fixed models, such as an 82.3% increase in F1-score on the TKG-Kernel dataset.

This note enhances and reinforces Nica's theory of robust shift equivalence for row-finite directed graphs and their associated C*-algebras. It introduces new evidence-based theorems that maintain the validity of Nica's theory under specific conditions. Furthermore, it establishes a more comprehensive classification system for row-finite directed graphs based on robust shift equivalence. At the level of C*-algebras, this classification system translates to a robust version of Morosawa-Pimoon-Tomforth theorem. The classification system also demonstrates that robust shift equivalence respects various subalgebra classifications within the C*-algebra framework.

Heavy heavy heavy quark pairwise interactions are investigated at finite magnetic fields and zero temperature within the quark gluon dual plasma framework. By employing an anisotropic magnetized Fermi gas model, we calculate the heavy quark distribution and obtain separation information through a shift in the heavy quark optical potential. Our analysis reveals how this separation changes in response to varying magnetic fields and anisotropy types.

Several systems have been developed to answer inquiries that blend multiple questions, but they typically rely on pre-built Knowledge Graphs and are limited in their ability to infer new relationships between entities. This work focuses on upgrading a dense vector-based language model with the ability to infer new connections in a Knowledge Graph, allowing it to make more informed decisions about inquiry answers. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by achieving a new state-of-the-art performance on the OpenDomain question answering challenge.

We introduce a novel high dimensional expansion from covers framework in this talk. It can be utilized to establish dimensional expansions in various contexts, including high dimensional bounded convex optimization and statistical inference. Furthermore, we utilize this framework to develop new attainment dimensions for supermodular maximization and demonstrate the achievement of optimal worst-case rates in supermodular minimization problems through the creation of a novel spherical cover.
